```tea
hline("overbought", 70.0, "Overbought", color=color.red, linestyle=hline.style_dashed)
```

**Output:**

```text
index  overbought
0      {"id":"overbought","price":70,"title":"Overbought","color":{"r":255,"g":82,"b":82,"a":255},"linestyle":"dashed","linewidth":1,"editable":true,"display":"all"}
```

**See also:** [`fill`](#fill), [`plot`](#plot)

entries.summary: Writes a shaded area between two plots or horizontal lines to a named output.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: Name of the output this call writes.

parameters.name: plot1
parameters.description: One edge of the area: the value returned by [`plot`](#plot) or [`hline`](#hline). Only its `id` is recorded.

parameters.name: color
parameters.description: Fill color on the current bar; it may change from bar to bar. `na` records no color, leaving the choice to the host.

parameters.name: editable
parameters.description: Whether users may edit the output's style in the host.

parameters.name: display
parameters.description: Where the output appears: a `display.*` constant such as [`display.all`](#display.*) or [`display.none`](#display.*).

entries.returns: `visual.Fill`: the description written to `id`; its `first` and `second` fields hold the IDs of `plot1` and `plot2`.
entries.body:
**Example:** A zone between two levels. The `zone` description names its edges by their
IDs, `upper` and `lower`.

```tea
upper = hline("upper", 70.0, "Upper")
lower = hline("lower", 30.0, "Lower")
fill("zone", upper, lower, color=color.new(color.blue, 90))
```

**Output:**

```text
index  upper                                                                                                                     lower                                                                                                                     zone
0      {"id":"upper","price":70,"title":"Upper","color":null,"linestyle":"solid","linewidth":1,"editable":true,"display":"all"}  {"id":"lower","price":30,"title":"Lower","color":null,"linestyle":"solid","linewidth":1,"editable":true,"display":"all"}  {"id":"zone","first":"upper","second":"lower","color":{"r":33,"g":150,"b":243,"a":26},"title":"","editable":true,"display":"all"}
```

**See also:** [`plot`](#plot), [`hline`](#hline)

entries.summary: Writes on each bar whether to show a shape marker there, with options for drawing it, to a named output.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: Name of the output this call writes.

parameters.name: series
parameters.description: Whether the shape appears on the current bar.

parameters.name: style
parameters.description: Shape to draw: a `shape.*` constant such as [`shape.circle`](#shape.*), [`shape.triangleup`](#shape.*) or [`shape.xcross`](#shape.*).

parameters.name: location
parameters.description: Where to place the shape: a `location.*` constant such as [`location.abovebar`](#location.*) or [`location.belowbar`](#location.*).

parameters.name: color
parameters.description: Shape color on the current bar; `na` records no color, leaving the choice to the host.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: Number of bars to shift the drawing by: a positive number moves it right, toward later bars, and a negative number left.

parameters.name: text
parameters.description: Text to show with the shape.

parameters.name: textcolor
parameters.description: Color of `text` on the current bar; `na` records no color, leaving the choice to the host.

parameters.name: size
parameters.description: Shape size: a `size.*` constant such as [`size.auto`](#size.*), [`size.small`](#size.*) or [`size.large`](#size.*).

parameters.name: editable
parameters.description: Whether users may edit the output's style in the host.

parameters.name: show_last
parameters.description: Number of most recent bars to draw; `0`, the default, sets no limit.

parameters.name: display
parameters.description: Where the output appears: a `display.*` constant such as [`display.all`](#display.*) or [`display.none`](#display.*).

parameters.name: force_overlay
parameters.description: Whether the host places this mark on the main price pane.

entries.returns: `visual.Shape`: the description written to `id`, with fields named after the parameters.
entries.body:
The description is written on every bar the call runs, not only where the
condition is true: its `series` field says whether the shape appears on
that bar.

**Example:** A triangle below each bar where the close crosses above `11`. Every bar
writes a description; `series` is `true` only at index 1.

```tea
emit "close" close
plotshape("cross", ta.crossover(close, 11.0), "Cross", style=shape.triangleup, location=location.belowbar)
```

```csv
time,close
0,10
1,12
2,13
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  cross
0      10     {"id":"cross","series":false,"title":"Cross","style":"triangleup","location":"belowbar","color":null,"offset":0,"text":"","textcolor":null,"size":"auto","editable":true,"show_last":0,"display":"all","force_overlay":false}
1      12     {"id":"cross","series":true,"title":"Cross","style":"triangleup","location":"belowbar","color":null,"offset":0,"text":"","textcolor":null,"size":"auto","editable":true,"show_last":0,"display":"all","force_overlay":false}
2      13     {"id":"cross","series":false,"title":"Cross","style":"triangleup","location":"belowbar","color":null,"offset":0,"text":"","textcolor":null,"size":"auto","editable":true,"show_last":0,"display":"all","force_overlay":false}
```

**See also:** [`plotchar`](#plotchar)

entries.summary: Writes on each bar whether to show a character marker there, with options for drawing it, to a named output.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: Name of the output this call writes.

parameters.name: series
parameters.description: Whether the character appears on the current bar.

parameters.name: location
parameters.description: Where to place the character: a `location.*` constant such as [`location.abovebar`](#location.*) or [`location.belowbar`](#location.*).

parameters.name: color
parameters.description: Character color on the current bar; `na` records no color, leaving the choice to the host.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: Number of bars to shift the drawing by: a positive number moves it right, toward later bars, and a negative number left.

parameters.name: text
parameters.description: Text to show with the character.

parameters.name: textcolor
parameters.description: Color of `text` on the current bar; `na` records no color, leaving the choice to the host.

parameters.name: size
parameters.description: Character size: a `size.*` constant such as [`size.auto`](#size.*), [`size.small`](#size.*) or [`size.large`](#size.*).

parameters.name: editable
parameters.description: Whether users may edit the output's style in the host.

parameters.name: show_last
parameters.description: Number of most recent bars to draw; `0`, the default, sets no limit.

parameters.name: display
parameters.description: Where the output appears: a `display.*` constant such as [`display.all`](#display.*) or [`display.none`](#display.*).

parameters.name: force_overlay
parameters.description: Whether the host places this mark on the main price pane.

entries.returns: `visual.Character`: the description written to `id`, with fields named after the parameters.
entries.body:
The description is written on every bar the call runs, not only where the
condition is true: its `series` field says whether the character appears on
that bar.

**Example:** A `+` above each bar whose close is higher than the one before. `series` is
`false` at index 0, where `close[1]` is `na`, and at index 2.

```tea
emit "close" close
plotchar("higher", close > close[1], "Higher", char="+")
```

```csv
time,close
0,10
1,12
2,11
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  higher
0      10     {"id":"higher","series":false,"title":"Higher","char":"+","location":"abovebar","color":null,"offset":0,"text":"","textcolor":null,"size":"auto","editable":true,"show_last":0,"display":"all","force_overlay":false}
1      12     {"id":"higher","series":true,"title":"Higher","char":"+","location":"abovebar","color":null,"offset":0,"text":"","textcolor":null,"size":"auto","editable":true,"show_last":0,"display":"all","force_overlay":false}
2      11     {"id":"higher","series":false,"title":"Higher","char":"+","location":"abovebar","color":null,"offset":0,"text":"","textcolor":null,"size":"auto","editable":true,"show_last":0,"display":"all","force_overlay":false}
```

**See also:** [`plotshape`](#plotshape)

entries.summary: Writes a background color for the current bar to a named output.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: Name of the output this call writes.

parameters.name: color
parameters.description: Background color on the current bar; `na` records no color.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: Number of bars to shift the drawing by: a positive number moves it right, toward later bars, and a negative number left.

parameters.name: editable

entries.summary: Writes a vertical profile, bands of the vertical axis drawn sideways inside a time box, to a named output.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: Name of the output this call writes.

parameters.name: from
parameters.description: Start of the box, as a time such as [`time`](#time).

parameters.name: rows
parameters.description: Bands of the profile, in any order; they must not overlap.

parameters.name: levels
parameters.description: Lines across the box, such as a point of control.

parameters.name: display
parameters.description: Where the output appears: a `display.*` constant such as [`display.all`](#display.*) or [`display.none`](#display.*).

entries.returns: The description written to `id`, with fields named after the parameters.
entries.body:
Each row is a band of the axis, such as a price range, drawn sideways from
`from` toward `to`; the longest row fills the box. A volume profile is one
use: one row per price range, its parts the volume traded on rising and on
falling bars. The host draws, for each `from`, only the description written
on the last row that carries it. Every row written is sent and kept, so
write a finished profile once and a forming one only while its bar can still
change. This draws one fixed two-row profile:

```tea
start = time[10]
rows = array.from(ProfileRow.new(100.0, 101.0, array.from(ProfileSegment.new(3.0, color.green))), ProfileRow.new(101.0, 102.0, array.from(ProfileSegment.new(1.0, color.red))))
levels = array.from(ProfileLevel.new(100.5, color.orange))
verticalProfile("profile", start, time, rows, levels, "Profile")
```

pages.title: Alerts
pages.description: Alert conditions and alert messages a host can deliver.
pages.intro:
Each call writes one named output that a host can deliver as an alert. See outputs and events.

Functions that describe plots, shapes, colors and alerts as named outputs.

Each plotting call records its arguments in a description value and writes
it to the output named by its first argument, `id`; each alert call appends
an event to the list named by `id`. Tea draws and sends nothing: the host
decides how to draw or deliver each output. Tea does not check the options
either: a style, line style, location, size, display or format name is
recorded as written, so a misspelled one is not an error, and numbers such
as `linewidth` are recorded even when negative. Only the script itself can
call these functions, not a library file.

A host recognizes each output by its type id: `visual.Plot` for
[`plot`](#plot), `visual.Hline` for [`hline`](#hline), `visual.Fill` for
[`fill`](#fill), `visual.Shape` for [`plotshape`](#plotshape), `visual.Character` for
[`plotchar`](#plotchar), `visual.Background` for [`bgcolor`](#bgcolor) and
`visual.BarColor` for [`barcolor`](#barcolor). An alert output is a list of
`visual.Alert` events for [`alertcondition`](#alertcondition), or of
`visual.AlertEvent<T>` events for [`alert`](#alert), where `T` is the type of
the alert's payload.

An `id` is a constant string, unique among the script's outputs; only alert
calls may share one. It cannot be empty or one of `index`, `time`, `timed`
and `provisional`. Apart from the alerts, a call may run at most once per
bar, so not inside a loop. On a bar where it does not run, such as inside
an `if` whose condition is false, its output is `null`, which `tea run`
prints as `na`. An alert output holds a list on every bar, `[]` when no
event was appended.

**Pine Script:** Every plot and alert function takes an output `id` first, so Pine
Script's `plot(ta.sma(close, 2))` fails with "missing argument 'series' in
call to 'plot'"; write `plot("sma", ta.sma(close, 2))`. Tea cannot create
drawing objects: there is no `label.new`, `line.new`, `box.new`,
`table.new`, `polyline.new` or `linefill.new`, so every value of the
`label`, `line`, `box`, `table`, `polyline` and `linefill` types is `na`.

Available in every script without an import or namespace.

entries.summary: Appends an alert event with fixed text on each bar where a condition is true.

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: Name of the event list this call appends to. Several `alertcondition` calls may share one `id`, and one call may run several times on a bar, as in a loop; the events keep the order in which the calls run.

parameters.name: condition
parameters.description: Whether to append an event on the current bar.

parameters.name: title
parameters.description: Event title; it cannot change from bar to bar.

parameters.name: message
parameters.description: Event message; it cannot change from bar to bar.

entries.returns: Nothing; use the call as a statement.
entries.body:
Each bar where `condition` is true appends one event with the fields `title`
and `message`, and the output `id` holds the bar's events as a list, `[]` on
a bar with none.
A condition that stays true appends an event on every bar, so pass a
transition such as [`ta.crossover`](#ta.crossover) to alert once per crossing. When
the host re-runs the current bar with live updates, each run writes only its
own events, replacing those of the earlier runs; combine the condition with
[`barstate.isconfirmed`](#barstate.isconfirmed) to append only on the bar's final run. Tea
sends no notification: the host decides what to do with each event.

**Example:** `above` appends an event on every bar whose close is above `11`, indexes 1,
2 and 4; `cross` appends only where the close crosses above `11`, indexes 1
and 4. A bar without an event holds `[]`.

```tea
emit "close" close
alertcondition("above", close > 11, "Above", "Close is above 11")
alertcondition("cross", ta.crossover(close, 11.0), "Cross", "Close crossed above 11")
```

```csv
time,close
0,10
1,12
2,13
3,10
4,12
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  above                                              cross
0      10     []                                                 []
1      12     [{"title":"Above","message":"Close is above 11"}]  [{"title":"Cross","message":"Close crossed above 11"}]
2      13     [{"title":"Above","message":"Close is above 11"}]  []
3      10     []                                                 []
4      12     [{"title":"Above","message":"Close is above 11"}]  [{"title":"Cross","message":"Close crossed above 11"}]
```

**See also:** [`alert`](#alert)

entries.summary: Appends an alert event with per-bar text and a struct payload on each bar where a condition is true.
signatures:
alert(
    const string id,
    series bool condition,
    series string title,
    series string message,
    data
)

parameters.name: id
parameters.description: Name of the event list this call appends to. Several `alert` calls may share one `id` when they pass the same `data` type; an `alertcondition` call cannot share it.

parameters.name: condition
parameters.description: Whether to append an event on the current bar.

parameters.name: title
parameters.description: Event title; may change from bar to bar.

parameters.name: message
parameters.description: Event message; may change from bar to bar.

parameters.name: data
parameters.description: Payload: any struct value, such as `Move.new(close, change)` in the example. Numbers, strings, arrays and other values that are not structs are rejected.

entries.returns: Nothing; use the call as a statement.
entries.body:
Each bar where `condition` is true appends one event with the fields
`title`, `message` and `data`, and the output `id` holds the bar's events as
a list, `[]` on a bar with none. Unlike [`alertcondition`](#alertcondition), the text can
change from bar to bar, and `data` carries a struct value whose fields keep
their types in the output. Repeated true bars and live re-runs behave as for
[`alertcondition`](#alertcondition).

**Example:** An event on each bar whose close moves by `2` or more, at indexes 1 and 3.
The message shows the move, and `data` keeps the struct's fields.

```tea
struct Move
    float price
    float change

emit "close" close
change = close - close[1]
alert("move", math.abs(change) >= 2, "Big move", "Close moved " + str.tostring(change), Move.new(close, change))
```

```csv
time,close
0,10
1,13
2,12
3,9
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  move
0      10     []
1      13     [{"title":"Big move","message":"Close moved 3","data":{"price":13,"change":3}}]
2      12     []
3      9      [{"title":"Big move","message":"Close moved -3","data":{"price":9,"change":-3}}]
```

**Pine Script:** Pine Script's `alert(message, freq)` has a different signature: it
takes no `id`, condition, title or payload, and Tea has no `freq` parameter
or `alert.freq_*` constants.

**See also:** [`alertcondition`](#alertcondition)

pages.title: ta
pages.description: Moving averages, oscillators, bands, crosses, pivots and volume indicators.
pages.intro:
Technical-analysis functions and variables: moving averages, oscillators, volatility bands, crosses, pivots, volume indicators and running statistics.

Each written call keeps its own history and state, covering only the bars on
which that call runs. A call does not run on a bar when the code around it
is skipped, such as an `if` branch, `switch` arm or ternary arm that is not
taken, the right side of an `and` or `or` whose left side already decides
the result, or a loop that runs zero times. Its windows then read that bar
as `na`, and its running state does not change on it. A call inside a loop
shares one history and state across all iterations, so its running state
advances on each iteration. Call these functions on every bar and combine
their results with conditions afterwards; see
values and control flow.

```tea
// Call on every bar, then combine the result with the condition.
risingThree = ta.rising(close, 3)
emit "signal" close > open and risingThree
```

The variables, such as [`ta.obv`](#ta.obv) and [`ta.wad`](#ta.wad), are not calls:
each is computed once per bar for the whole script, so every read sees the
same value, even one inside an `if`.

A window function reads the last `length` bars of its source and leaves out
the `na` values among them. When none is left, the result is `na`, or
`false` for [`ta.rising`](#ta.rising) and [`ta.falling`](#ta.falling). In [`ta.alma`](#ta.alma),
[`ta.linreg`](#ta.linreg), [`ta.percentrank`](#ta.percentrank) and [`ta.swma`](#ta.swma), an `na` value
anywhere in the window makes the result `na` instead, and [`ta.change`](#ta.change),
[`ta.mom`](#ta.mom) and [`ta.roc`](#ta.roc) are `na` when either value they compare is
`na`. [`ta.cci`](#ta.cci), [`ta.stoch`](#ta.stoch) and [`ta.wpr`](#ta.wpr) are `na`, and
[`ta.rising`](#ta.rising) and [`ta.falling`](#ta.falling) are `false`, when the current value
they measure is `na`. Most results are also `na` until enough bars have
arrived; each entry says when.

Most sources are typed `float`: an `int` source, such as [`bar_index`](#bar_index),
is converted to `float`, and a `bool` or `string` source is a compile error.
[`ta.change`](#ta.change) keeps an `int` source `int`. A `simple` parameter, such as
the `length` of [`ta.ema`](#ta.ema), takes a value known when the script starts,
like a constant or an input; a `series` value, such as `bar_index + 1`, is a
compile error there.

A count, such as `length`, has a minimum, which its parameter states. A
value below it, or `na`, stops the run with an error that names the
function, such as `ta.sma: length must be at least 1`; a constant that low,
or `na`, is a compile error at the call. A `series` length, such as
`bar_index + 1`, reaches back at most 500 bars: older values read as `na`.
A constant or input length is not limited this way.

**Pine Script:** These differences apply across `ta`:

- Not in Tea yet: `ta.median`, `ta.mode`,
  `ta.percentile_linear_interpolation`, `ta.percentile_nearest_rank`,
  `ta.pivot_point_levels`, `ta.rci`, `ta.valuewhen`, `ta.vwap` (the function
  and the variable) and the variable `ta.tr`, which Tea writes as the call
  `ta.tr(false)`.
- The Pine manual states no minimum for counts such as `length`; in Tea a
  count below its minimum, such as a `length` of `0`, or an `na` count is an
  error.
- The Pine manual says that `na` values are ignored, and for some functions
  that the calculation uses `length` values that are not `na`. A Tea window
  function reads the last `length` bars and leaves out the `na` values among
  them, so it can use fewer than `length` values.

Available in every script as `ta.name` without an import.

entries.summary: Simple moving average: the mean of the last `length` values of `source`.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of bars in the window, at least 1.

entries.returns: `float`: the mean of the window.
entries.body:
Every value in the window has the same weight. Values that are `na` are
left out, so the mean is over the window's other values.

**Formula**

$$
\mathrm{sma}_t = \frac{1}{|K_t|} \sum_{i \in K_t} \mathit{source}_{t-i}
\quad\text{where}\quad
K_t = \{\, i : 0 \le i < \mathit{length},
\ \mathit{source}_{t-i} \ne \text{na} \,\}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` on the first `length - 1` bars, and when every value in the
window is `na`.

**Example:** A 3-bar average. The first two bars are `na`. The close is missing at
index 4, so the windows that hold it average their two known values.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "sma" ta.sma(close, 3)
```

```csv
time,close
0,10
1,11
2,12
3,13
4,
5,15
6,16
7,17
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  sma
0      10     na
1      11     na
2      12     11
3      13     12
4      na     12.5
5      15     14
6      16     15.5
7      17     16
```

**See also:** [`ta.ema`](#ta.ema), [`ta.wma`](#ta.wma)

entries.summary: Exponential moving average of `source`: a running average that gives recent values more weight.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Smoothing length in bars, at least 1; larger values react more slowly. It must be known when the script starts, such as a constant or an input.

entries.returns: `float`: the average.
entries.body:
Each bar moves the average toward `source` by `2 / (length + 1)` of the
difference, so the weight of older values falls off exponentially. The
average starts at the first value of `source` that is not `na`, without
waiting for `length` bars, and a bar where `source` is `na` leaves it
unchanged. [`ta.rma`](#ta.rma) moves by `1 / length` instead and waits for
`length` values.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{ema}_t &= \begin{cases}
\mathrm{ema}_{t-1} & \text{if } \mathit{source}_t = \text{na} \\
\mathit{source}_t & \text{if } \mathrm{ema}_{t-1} = \text{na} \\
\alpha \cdot \mathit{source}_t + (1 - \alpha) \cdot \mathrm{ema}_{t-1}
& \text{otherwise}
\end{cases} \\
\text{where}\quad \alpha &= \frac{2}{\mathit{length} + 1}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` until the first bar where `source` is not `na`. After that it
is never `na`: a bar where `source` is `na` keeps the previous result.

**Example:** A 3-bar average moves half of the way, `2 / (3 + 1)`, toward each close.
It is `na` before the first close and starts at that close, 10 at index 1.
The missing close at index 5 keeps the previous value, 13.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "ema" ta.ema(close, 3)
```

```csv
time,close
0,
1,10
2,12
3,11
4,15
5,
6,17
7,19
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  ema
0      na     na
1      10     10
2      12     11
3      11     11
4      15     13
5      na     13
6      17     15
7      19     17
```

**See also:** [`ta.rma`](#ta.rma), [`ta.sma`](#ta.sma)

entries.summary: Wilder's smoothed moving average of `source`, the running average behind [`ta.rsi`](#ta.rsi), [`ta.atr`](#ta.atr) and [`ta.dmi`](#ta.dmi).

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Smoothing length in bars, at least 1; also the number of values in the starting mean. It must be known when the script starts, such as a constant or an input.

entries.returns: `float`: the average.
entries.body:
It starts at the mean of the first `length` values of `source` that are not
`na`, then moves toward each new value by `1 / length` of the difference. A
bar where `source` is `na` is skipped: it does not count toward the first
`length` values, and later it keeps the previous result. [`ta.ema`](#ta.ema)
moves by `2 / (length + 1)` instead and starts at the first value.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{rma}_t &= \begin{cases}
\text{na} & \text{if } c_t < \mathit{length} \\
\dfrac{1}{\mathit{length}}
\displaystyle\sum_{i \in K_t} \mathit{source}_{t-i}
& \text{if } c_{t-1} < c_t = \mathit{length} \\
\mathrm{rma}_{t-1} & \text{if } \mathit{source}_t = \text{na} \\
\alpha \cdot \mathit{source}_t + (1 - \alpha) \cdot \mathrm{rma}_{t-1}
& \text{otherwise}
\end{cases} \\
\text{where}\quad
K_t &= \{\, i \ge 0 : \mathit{source}_{t-i} \ne \text{na} \,\},
\quad c_t = |K_t|,
\quad \alpha = \frac{1}{\mathit{length}}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` until `length` values of `source` that are not `na` have
arrived, on consecutive bars or not. After that it is never `na`: a bar
where `source` is `na` keeps the previous result.

**Example:** A 3-bar average. The close at index 1 is missing, so the third value
arrives at index 3, where the average starts at `(10 + 12 + 14) / 3 = 12`.
Each later close moves it a third of the way, and the missing close at
index 5 keeps 14.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "rma" ta.rma(close, 3)
```

```csv
time,close
0,10
1,
2,12
3,14
4,18
5,
6,20
7,22
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  rma
0      10     na
1      na     na
2      12     na
3      14     12
4      18     14
5      na     14
6      20     16
7      22     18
```

**See also:** [`ta.ema`](#ta.ema), [`ta.rsi`](#ta.rsi)

entries.summary: Weighted moving average: the mean of the last `length` values of `source`, with weights falling linearly from the newest value to the oldest.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of bars in the window, at least 1.

entries.returns: `float`: the weighted mean of the window.
entries.body:
The newest value has weight `length`, the one before it `length - 1`, and so
on down to 1 for the oldest, and the weighted sum is divided by the sum of
the weights. Values that are `na` are left out together with their weights.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{wma}_t &= \frac
{\sum_{i \in K_t} (\mathit{length} - i) \cdot \mathit{source}_{t-i}}
{\sum_{i \in K_t} (\mathit{length} - i)} \\
\text{where}\quad K_t &= \{\, i : 0 \le i < \mathit{length},
\ \mathit{source}_{t-i} \ne \text{na} \,\}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` on the first `length - 1` bars, and when every value in the
window is `na`.

**Example:** A 3-bar average weights the closes 3, 2 and 1 from newest to oldest, so at
index 2 it is `(3 * 16 + 2 * 13 + 10) / 6 = 14`. The close at index 4 is
missing, so at index 5 only the weights 3 and 1 remain:
`(3 * 25 + 19) / 4 = 23.5`.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "wma" ta.wma(close, 3)
```

```csv
time,close
0,10
1,13
2,16
3,19
4,
5,25
6,28
7,31
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  wma
0      10     na
1      13     na
2      16     14
3      19     17
4      na     18
5      25     23.5
6      28     26.8
7      31     29
```

**See also:** [`ta.sma`](#ta.sma), [`ta.hma`](#ta.hma)

entries.summary: Volume-weighted moving average: the mean of the last `length` values of `source`, each weighted by its bar's [`volume`](#volume).

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of bars in the window, at least 1.

entries.returns: `float`: the weighted mean of the window.
entries.body:
It is the sum of `source * volume` divided by the sum of `volume`, over the
bars in the window where neither is `na`.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{vwma}_t &= \frac
{\sum_{i \in K_t} \mathit{source}_{t-i} \cdot \mathit{volume}_{t-i}}
{\sum_{i \in K_t} \mathit{volume}_{t-i}} \\
\text{where}\quad
K_t &= \{\, i : 0 \le i < \mathit{length},
\ \mathit{source}_{t-i} \ne \text{na},
\ \mathit{volume}_{t-i} \ne \text{na} \,\}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` on the first `length - 1` bars, when no bar in the window has
both `source` and `volume`, and when the volumes of the bars used add up
to 0.

**Example:** A 3-bar average. At index 3 it is
`(12 * 300 + 11 * 100 + 14 * 200) / 600 = 12.5`. The close at index 4 is
missing, so that bar's volume is left out too: at index 4 the result is
`(11 * 100 + 14 * 200) / 300 = 13`.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "volume" volume
emit "vwma" ta.vwma(close, 3)
```

```csv
time,close,volume
0,10,100
1,12,300
2,11,100
3,14,200
4,,300
5,16,200
6,19,100
7,21,100
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  volume  vwma
0      10     100     na
1      12     300     na
2      11     100     11.4
3      14     200     12.5
4      na     300     13
5      16     200     15
6      19     100     17
7      21     100     18
```

**Pine Script:** Pine's manual defines it as
`ta.sma(source * volume, length) / ta.sma(volume, length)`. The two differ
when `source` is `na` on a bar whose volume is known: Tea leaves that
volume out, while `ta.sma(volume, length)` still counts it.

**See also:** [`ta.sma`](#ta.sma), [`ta.wma`](#ta.wma)

entries.summary: Hull moving average of `source`, built from three [`ta.wma`](#ta.wma) averages to reduce lag.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of bars in the longest of the three averages, at least 2. It must be known when the script starts, such as a constant or an input.

entries.returns: `float`: the average.
entries.body:
It is a [`ta.wma`](#ta.wma) over `math.floor(math.sqrt(length))` bars of
`2 * ta.wma(source, length / 2) - ta.wma(source, length)`, with
`length / 2` rounded down. Each of the three averages leaves out `na`
values.

The difference first exists on the bar where `ta.wma(source, length)`
fills, and the result waits until the outer average holds
`math.floor(math.sqrt(length))` differences, so it starts
`math.floor(math.sqrt(length)) - 1` bars after `ta.wma(source, length)`:
at index 8 rather than 7 for a `length` of 8. The formula applies from
then on.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{hma}_t &= \mathrm{wma}(d, r)_t \\
d_t &= 2 \cdot \mathrm{wma}(\mathit{source}, h)_t
- \mathrm{wma}(\mathit{source}, \mathit{length})_t \\
\text{where}\quad h &= \lfloor \mathit{length} / 2 \rfloor,
\quad r = \lfloor \sqrt{\mathit{length}} \rfloor
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` on the first `length + math.floor(math.sqrt(length)) - 2`
bars: 4 for a `length` of 4, 10 for 9. After that, `na` values are left
out, and the result is `na` only while the last
`math.floor(length / 2) + math.floor(math.sqrt(length)) - 1` values of
`source` are all `na`: 3 for a `length` of 4, 6 for 9.

**Example:** With a `length` of 4 the first value is at index
`4 + math.floor(math.sqrt(4)) - 2 = 4`. While the closes rise by 1 a bar it
equals the close. The close at index 8 is missing; the averages leave it
out, so the result there is still a number.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "hma" ta.hma(close, 4)
```

```csv

0,10
1,11
2,12
3,13
4,14
5,15
6,16
7,15
8,
9,13
10,12
```

**Output:**

```text

0      10     na
1      11     na
2      12     na
3      13     na
4      14     14
5      15     15
6      16     16
7      15     15.755555555555555
8      na     14.933333333333332
9      13     12.888888888888888
10     12     11.944444444444445
```

**See also:** [`ta.wma`](#ta.wma), [`ta.ema`](#ta.ema)

entries.summary: Symmetrically weighted moving average: the mean of the last four values of `source`, with weights 1, 2, 2 and 1.
entries.returns: `float`: the weighted mean of the four values.
entries.body:
The weights are 1/6, 2/6, 2/6 and 1/6 from the oldest value to the newest.
The window is always four bars; there is no `length` parameter. An `na`
value in the window makes the result `na`.

**Formula**

$$
\mathrm{swma}_t = \frac
{\mathit{source}_{t-3} + 2 \cdot \mathit{source}_{t-2}
+ 2 \cdot \mathit{source}_{t-1} + \mathit{source}_t}
{6}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` on the first 3 bars, and while any of the four values is
`na`.

**Example:** The first value is at index 3: `(12 + 2 * 12 + 2 * 18 + 18) / 6 = 15`. The
close at index 7 is missing, so the four windows that hold it, at indexes 7
to 10, are `na`.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "swma" ta.swma(close)
```

```text
8      18     na
9      24     na
10     24     na
11     18     22
```

**See also:** [`ta.wma`](#ta.wma), [`ta.sma`](#ta.sma)

entries.summary: Arnaud Legoux moving average: the mean of the last `length` values of `series`, weighted by a bell curve.
signatures:
ta.alma(
    float series,
    int length,
    simple float offset,
    simple float sigma,
    simple bool floor = false
)

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of bars in the window, at least 1.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: Position of the peak weight, from 0 (the oldest value) to 1 (the newest). It must be known when the script starts, such as a constant or an input.

parameters.name: sigma
parameters.description: Sharpness of the curve: its standard deviation is `length / sigma` bars, so a larger `sigma` puts more of the weight near the peak. It must be known when the script starts, such as a constant or an input.

parameters.name: floor
parameters.description: `true` rounds the peak position down to a whole bar; `false`, the default, keeps it as computed. It must be known when the script starts, such as a constant or an input.

entries.returns: `float`: the weighted mean of the window.
entries.body:
The weights follow a Gaussian curve across the window. Its peak sits
`offset * (length - 1)` positions after the oldest value, and its standard
deviation is `length / sigma` bars. The weighted sum is divided by the sum
of the weights. An `na` value in the window makes the result `na`.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{alma}_t &= \frac
{\sum_{j=0}^{\mathit{length}-1} w_j
\cdot \mathit{series}_{t-\mathit{length}+1+j}}
{\sum_{j=0}^{\mathit{length}-1} w_j},
\qquad w_j = \exp\left(-\frac{(j - m)^2}{2 s^2}\right) \\
\text{where}\quad m &= \begin{cases}
\lfloor \mathit{offset} \cdot (\mathit{length} - 1) \rfloor
& \text{if } \mathit{floor} \\
\mathit{offset} \cdot (\mathit{length} - 1) & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases},
\qquad s = \frac{\mathit{length}}{\mathit{sigma}}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` on the first `length - 1` bars, and while any value in the
window is `na`.

**Example:** Over 4 bars with `offset` 0.85, the peak sits at position 2.55, between the
two newest closes. `floor = true` moves it back to position 2, so older
closes weigh more; as these closes trend up, the floored average is lower
on every bar that has a value. The close at index 6 is missing, so indexes
6 to 9 are `na`.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "alma" ta.alma(close, 4, 0.85, 6)
emit "floored" ta.alma(close, 4, 0.85, 6, true)
```

```csv
3,15
4,14
5,18
6,

8,20
9,22
10,21
11,24
```

```text
4      14     14.323177377953208  14.002303404456248
5      18     16.06290567122777   14.957553605910393
6      na     na                  na
7      17     na                  na
8      20     na                  na

11     24     22.5583412611759    21.77540958230943
```

**See also:** [`ta.wma`](#ta.wma), [`ta.sma`](#ta.sma)

entries.summary: Linear regression curve: the value of the least-squares line through the last `length` values of `source`, read `offset` bars back.
signatures: ta.linreg(float source, int length, simple int offset)

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of bars in the window, at least 2.

parameters.name: offset
parameters.description: Bars back from the current bar at which to read the line; 0 reads it on the current bar. It must be known when the script starts, such as a constant or an input.

entries.returns: `float`: the value of the fitted line.
entries.body:
The line is fitted with the oldest value at position 0 and the current
value at position `length - 1`, then read at position
`length - 1 - offset`. An `offset` of 0 gives the line's value on the
current bar, also known as the least-squares moving average, and a negative
`offset` extends the line past it. An `na` value in the window makes the
result `na`.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{linreg}_t &= a + b \cdot (n - 1 - \mathit{offset}) \\
b &= \frac
{n \sum_j j \cdot y_j - \left(\sum_j j\right) \left(\sum_j y_j\right)}
{n \sum_j j^2 - \left(\sum_j j\right)^2},
\qquad a = \frac{\sum_j y_j - b \sum_j j}{n} \\
\text{where}\quad n &= \mathit{length},
\quad y_j = \mathit{source}_{t-n+1+j},
\quad j = 0, \dots, n - 1
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` on the first `length - 1` bars, and while any value in the
window is `na`.

**Example:** At index 2 the closes 10, 14 and 12, at positions 0 to 2, fit the line
`11 + position`. It reads 13 on the current bar (`offset` 0) and 14 one bar
ahead (`offset` -1). The close at index 6 is missing, so indexes 6 to 8 are
`na`.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "fit" ta.linreg(close, 3, 0)
emit "ahead" ta.linreg(close, 3, -1)
```

```csv
0,10
1,14
2,12
3,16
4,20
5,18
6,
7,22
8,26
9,24
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  fit  ahead
0      10     na   na
1      14     na   na
2      12     13   14
3      16     15   16
4      20     20   24
5      18     19   20
6      na     na   na
7      22     na   na
8      26     na   na
9      24     25   26
```

**See also:** [`ta.sma`](#ta.sma), [`ta.correlation`](#ta.correlation)

entries.summary: Center of gravity (COG) of the last `length` values of `source`.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of bars in the window, at least 1.

entries.returns: `float`: the center of gravity.
entries.body:
It is minus the average bar position in the window, from `1` for the
current bar to `length` for the oldest, with each position weighted by its
value. Values that are `na` are left out, and the others keep their
positions. For positive values it lies between `-length` and `-1`:
`length` equal values give `-(length + 1) / 2`, and larger newer values
move it toward `-1`.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{cog}_t &= -\frac{\sum_{i \in K_t} (i + 1) \cdot \mathit{source}_{t-i}}
{\sum_{i \in K_t} \mathit{source}_{t-i}} \\
\text{where}\quad K_t &= \{\, i : 0 \le i < \mathit{length},
\ \mathit{source}_{t-i} \ne \text{na} \,\}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` on the first `length - 1` bars, when every value in the window
is `na`, and when the known values sum to `0`.

**Example:** Equal closes give -2 at index 2, and the 20 moves the value to -1.75 while
it is newest (index 3) and to -2.25 while it is oldest (index 5). At index 6
the missing close is left out: `-(2 * 10 + 3 * 10) / 20` is -2.5.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "cog" ta.cog(close, 3)
```

```csv
time,close
0,10
1,10
2,10
3,20
4,10
5,10
6,
7,10
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  cog
0      10     na
1      10     na
2      10     -2
3      20     -1.75
4      10     -2
5      10     -2.25
6      na     -2.5
7      10     -2
```

**See also:** [`ta.wma`](#ta.wma), [`ta.stoch`](#ta.stoch)

entries.summary: Difference between `source` and its value `length` bars ago.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of bars back, at least 1. Leaving it out compares with the previous bar.

entries.returns: `float`, or `int` for an `int` source: the difference.
entries.body:
**Formula**

$$
\mathrm{change}_t = \mathit{source}_t - \mathit{source}_{t-\mathit{length}}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` on the first `length` bars, and when either value is `na`.

**Example:** The change from the previous bar and from two bars back. The close is
missing at index 4, so `change` is `na` at indexes 4 and 5, and `change2` at
indexes 4 and 6.

```tea

emit "change" ta.change(close)
emit "change2" ta.change(close, 2)
```

```csv
0,10
1,12
2,15
3,14
```

```text
1      12     2       na
2      15     3       5
3      14     -1      2
4      na     na      na
5      18     na      4
6      20     2       na
```

**Pine Script:** Pine also accepts a `bool` source, returning `true` when it differs
from the previous one; in Tea a `bool` source is a compile error.

**See also:** [`ta.mom`](#ta.mom), [`ta.roc`](#ta.roc)

entries.summary: Momentum: `source` minus its value `length` bars ago.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of bars back, at least 1.

entries.returns: `float`: the difference.
entries.body:
It is the same as [`ta.change`](#ta.change) with `length` required, except that an
`int` source gives a `float` result.

**Formula**

$$
\mathrm{mom}_t = \mathit{source}_t - \mathit{source}_{t-\mathit{length}}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` on the first `length` bars, and when either value is `na`.

**Example:** Momentum over 3 bars. The first value, at index 3, is `14 - 10`.

```tea

emit "mom" ta.mom(close, 3)
```

**See also:** [`ta.change`](#ta.change), [`ta.roc`](#ta.roc)

entries.summary: Rate of change (ROC): the percentage change of `source` from its value `length` bars ago.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of bars back, at least 1.

entries.returns: `float`: the change as a percentage of the earlier value.
entries.body:
**Formula**

$$
\mathrm{roc}_t = 100 \cdot
\frac{\mathit{source}_t - \mathit{source}_{t-\mathit{length}}}
{\mathit{source}_{t-\mathit{length}}}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` on the first `length` bars, when either value is `na`, and
when the earlier value is `0`.

**Example:** The rate of change over 2 bars: from 10 to 25 is 150 at index 2. The close
two bars before index 6 is 0, so that value is `na`.

```tea

emit "roc" ta.roc(close, 2)
```

```csv
1,20
2,25
3,30
4,0
5,15
6,40
7,30
```

```text

1      20     na
2      25     150
3      30     50
4      0      -100
5      15     -50
6      40     na
7      30     100
```

**See also:** [`ta.change`](#ta.change), [`ta.mom`](#ta.mom)

entries.summary: Relative Strength Index (RSI) of `source`, from `0` to `100`.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Smoothing length in bars, at least 1. It must be a value known when the script starts, such as a constant or an input.

entries.returns: `float`: the index.
entries.body:
The gains and the losses from bar to bar are each smoothed with
[`ta.rma`](#ta.rma) over `length` bars, and the index compares the two. It is
`100` when the smoothed loss is `0`, including on a flat series, and `0`
when only the smoothed gain is `0`.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta_t &= \mathit{source}_t - \mathit{source}_{t-1} \\
U_t &= \mathrm{rma}(\max(\Delta, 0), \mathit{length})_t \\
D_t &= \mathrm{rma}(\max(-\Delta, 0), \mathit{length})_t \\
\mathrm{rsi}_t &= \begin{cases}
100 & D_t = 0 \\
0 & U_t = 0,\ D_t > 0 \\
100 - \dfrac{100}{1 + U_t / D_t} & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` until `length` changes of `source` are known: the first
`length` bars when no value is `na`. An `na` value leaves out the changes
into and out of it, so once started the index keeps its value on that bar
and the next.

**Example:** A 3-bar RSI starts at index 3, where the average gain is `(2 + 0 + 2) / 3`
and the average loss `1 / 3`, giving 80. The close is missing at index 6,
so the index keeps its value there and at index 7.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "rsi" ta.rsi(close, 3)
```

```csv
time,close
0,10
1,12
2,11
3,13
4,13
5,12
6,
7,14
8,16
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  rsi
0      10     na
1      12     na
2      11     na
3      13     80
4      13     80
5      12     55.17241379310345
6      na     55.17241379310345
7      14     55.17241379310345
8      16     76.78571428571428
```

**See also:** [`ta.rma`](#ta.rma), [`ta.cmo`](#ta.cmo), [`ta.mfi`](#ta.mfi)

entries.summary: Chande Momentum Oscillator (CMO) of `series`, from `-100` to `100`.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of bar-to-bar changes in the window, at least 1.

entries.returns: `float`: the oscillator.
entries.body:
Over the last `length` bar-to-bar changes, it is the sum of the gains minus
the sum of the losses, as a percentage of their total. A change that
involves an `na` value is left out.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta_t &= \mathit{series}_t - \mathit{series}_{t-1} \\
K_t &= \{\, i : 0 \le i < \mathit{length},\
\Delta_{t-i} \ne \text{na} \,\} \\
G_t &= \sum_{i \in K_t} \max(\Delta_{t-i}, 0), \qquad
L_t = \sum_{i \in K_t} \max(-\Delta_{t-i}, 0) \\
\mathrm{cmo}_t &= 100 \cdot \frac{G_t - L_t}{G_t + L_t}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` on the first `length` bars, when no change in the window is
known, and when every known change is `0`.

**Example:** At index 2 a gain of 2 and a loss of 1 give `100 * (2 - 1) / (2 + 1)`. The
missing close at index 6 leaves out the changes into and out of it, so
index 7 has none left and is `na`.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "cmo" ta.cmo(close, 2)
```

```csv
time,close
0,10
1,12
2,11
3,11
4,14
5,13
6,
7,15
8,17
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  cmo
0      10     na
1      12     na
2      11     33.333333333333336
3      11     -100
4      14     100
5      13     50
6      na     -100
7      15     na
8      17     100
```

**See also:** [`ta.rsi`](#ta.rsi), [`ta.tsi`](#ta.tsi)

entries.summary: True Strength Index (TSI) of `source`, from `-1` to `1`.
signatures:
ta.tsi(
    float source,
    simple int short_length,
    simple int long_length
)

parameters.name: short_length
parameters.description: Length of the second smoothing in bars, at least 1. It must be a value known when the script starts, such as a constant or an input.

parameters.name: long_length
parameters.description: Length of the first smoothing in bars, at least 1. It must be a value known when the script starts, such as a constant or an input.

entries.returns: `float`: the index.
entries.body:
The bar-to-bar change of `source` is smoothed twice with [`ta.ema`](#ta.ema),
first over `long_length` bars and then over `short_length` bars, and divided
by the absolute change smoothed the same way. Both smoothings skip a bar
whose change is `na`.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta_t &= \mathit{source}_t - \mathit{source}_{t-1} \\
(a_t, b_t) &= \begin{cases}
\bigl(\mathrm{ema}(\Delta, \mathit{long\_length})_t,\
\mathrm{ema}(|\Delta|, \mathit{long\_length})_t\bigr)
& \Delta_t \ne \text{na} \\
(\text{na}, \text{na}) & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases} \\
\mathrm{tsi}_t &= \frac{\mathrm{ema}(a, \mathit{short\_length})_t}
{\mathrm{ema}(b, \mathit{short\_length})_t}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` until a bar-to-bar change of `source` is known and not `0`;
that change gives exactly `1` or `-1`. With both lengths `1`, it is also
`na` on each bar where `source` did not change. An `na` value leaves out
the changes into and out of it, so the index keeps its value on that bar
and the next.

**Example:** The first change gives 1 at index 1, and at index 2 the smoothed change, 1,
over the smoothed absolute change, `5 / 3`, gives 0.6. The close is missing
at index 5, so the index keeps its value there and at index 6.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "tsi" ta.tsi(close, 2, 3)
```

```csv
time,close
0,10
1,12
2,11
3,14
4,13
5,
6,16
7,15
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  tsi
0      10     na
1      12     1
2      11     0.6
3      14     0.7297297297297296
4      13     0.42408376963350786
5      na     0.42408376963350786
6      16     0.42408376963350786
7      15     0.02845100105374079
```

**See also:** [`ta.ema`](#ta.ema), [`ta.cmo`](#ta.cmo)

entries.summary: Stochastic oscillator, the fast %K: where `source` sits between the lowest `l` and the highest `h` of the last `length` bars, from `0` to `100`.
signatures: ta.stoch(float source, float h, float l, int length)

parameters.name: source
parameters.description: Series to place in the range, usually [`close`](#close).

parameters.name: h
parameters.description: Series whose highest value is the top of the range, usually [`high`](#high).

parameters.name: l
parameters.description: Series whose lowest value is the bottom of the range, usually [`low`](#low).

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of bars in the window, at least 1.

entries.returns: `float`: the position as a percentage of the range.
entries.body:
It uses [`ta.lowest`](#ta.lowest) and [`ta.highest`](#ta.highest), and leaves `0` to `100`
only when `source` lies outside that range. The result is not smoothed:
pass it to [`ta.sma`](#ta.sma) for the slow %K.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{stoch}_t &= 100 \cdot \frac{\mathit{source}_t - L_t}{H_t - L_t} \\
\text{where}\quad H_t &= \mathrm{highest}(\mathit{h}, \mathit{length})_t \\
L_t &= \mathrm{lowest}(\mathit{l}, \mathit{length})_t
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` on the first `length - 1` bars, when `source` is `na`, when a
window has no known value, and when the range is `0`. Other `na` values are
left out of the windows.

**Example:** At index 2 the close of 10 is 3 above the lowest low, 7, in a range of 5,
giving 60. The missing low at index 3 is left out of the windows, and the
missing close at index 4 makes that bar `na`.

```tea
emit "high" high
emit "low" low
emit "close" close
emit "stoch" ta.stoch(close, high, low, 3)
```

```csv
time,high,low,close
0,10,8,9
1,12,9,11
2,11,7,10
3,13,,12
4,12,8,
5,15,10,14
6,14,9,10
7,16,11,15
```

**Output:**

```text
index  high  low  close  stoch
0      10    8    9      na
1      12    9    11     na
2      11    7    10     60
3      13    na   12     83.33333333333333
4      12    8    na     na
5      15    10   14     85.71428571428571
6      14    9    10     28.571428571428573
7      16    11   15     85.71428571428571
```

**Pine Script:** Pine names the second and third parameters `high` and `low`; Tea names
them `h` and `l`, so named arguments read `h = high, l = low`.

**See also:** [`ta.wpr`](#ta.wpr), [`ta.highest`](#ta.highest), [`ta.lowest`](#ta.lowest)

entries.summary: Commodity Channel Index (CCI) of `source`.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of bars in the window, at least 1.

entries.returns: `float`: the index.
entries.body:
It is `source` minus its [`ta.sma`](#ta.sma), divided by `0.015` times the mean
absolute deviation ([`ta.dev`](#ta.dev)) of the same window. Values that are
`na` are left out of both.

**Formula**

$$
\mathrm{cci}_t = \frac{
\mathit{source}_t - \mathrm{sma}(\mathit{source}, \mathit{length})_t}
{0.015 \cdot \mathrm{dev}(\mathit{source}, \mathit{length})_t}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` on the first `length - 1` bars, when `source` is `na`, and when
the known values in the window are all equal, as they always are for a
`length` of 1.

**Example:** At index 2 the close is 1 above the 3-bar mean of 11 and the mean deviation
is `2 / 3`, giving about 100. Index 5 has no close, and from index 7 the
known closes in the window are equal, so those bars are `na`.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "cci" ta.cci(close, 3)
```

```csv
time,close
0,10
1,11
2,12
3,12
4,9
5,
6,12
7,12
8,12
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  cci
0      10     na
1      11     na
2      12     100.00000000000001
3      12     50.000000000000064
4      9      -100.00000000000001
5      na     na
6      12     66.66666666666667
7      12     na
8      12     na
```

**See also:** [`ta.sma`](#ta.sma), [`ta.dev`](#ta.dev)

entries.summary: Williams %R: where [`close`](#close) sits within the range of the last `length` bars, from `-100` to `0`.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of bars in the window, at least 1.

entries.returns: `float`: the position as a percentage of the range.
entries.body:
It is the position that [`ta.stoch`](#ta.stoch) measures, shifted down by `100`:
`0` when the close is at the highest [`high`](#high) of the window and `-100`
when it is at the lowest [`low`](#low). It leaves `-100` to `0` only when the
close lies outside that range.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\%R_t &= 100 \cdot \frac{\mathit{close}_t - H_t}{H_t - L_t} \\
\text{where}\quad H_t &= \mathrm{highest}(\mathit{high}, \mathit{length})_t \\
L_t &= \mathrm{lowest}(\mathit{low}, \mathit{length})_t
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` on the first `length - 1` bars, when [`close`](#close) is `na`,
when a window has no known value, and when the range is `0`. Other `na`
values are left out of the windows.

**Example:** A 3-bar %R. At index 2 the close of 10 is 2 below the highest high, 12, in
a range of 5, giving -40. The high is missing at index 3, so that window's
highest high is 12, and the close of 12 gives 0.

```tea
emit "high" high
emit "low" low
emit "close" close
emit "wpr" ta.wpr(3)
```

```csv
time,high,low,close
0,10,8,9
1,12,9,11
2,11,7,10
3,,9,12
4,12,8,9
5,15,10,14
6,14,9,10
```

**Output:**

```text
index  high  low  close  wpr
0      10    8    9      na
1      12    9    11     na
2      11    7    10     -40
3      na    9    12     0
4      12    8    9      -60
5      15    10   14     -14.285714285714286
6      14    9    10     -71.42857142857143
```

**See also:** [`ta.stoch`](#ta.stoch), [`ta.highest`](#ta.highest), [`ta.lowest`](#ta.lowest)

entries.summary: Money Flow Index (MFI) of `series`, from `0` to `100`.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of bars in the window, at least 1.

entries.returns: `float`: the index.
entries.body:
Each bar's money flow is `series` times [`volume`](#volume). Over the last
`length` bars, the flows of bars where `series` rose and of bars where it
fell are summed separately, and the index compares the two. A bar whose
change or flow involves an `na` value is left out, and a bar where `series`
did not change counts toward neither sum.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta_t &= \mathit{series}_t - \mathit{series}_{t-1}, \qquad
F_t = \mathit{series}_t \cdot \mathit{volume}_t \\
K_t &= \{\, i : 0 \le i < \mathit{length},\
\Delta_{t-i} \ne \text{na},\ F_{t-i} \ne \text{na} \,\} \\
P_t &= \sum_{i \in K_t,\ \Delta_{t-i} > 0} F_{t-i}, \qquad
N_t = \sum_{i \in K_t,\ \Delta_{t-i} < 0} F_{t-i} \\
\mathrm{mfi}_t &= 100 - \frac{100}{1 + P_t / N_t}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` on the first `length` bars, and when the bars in the window
that fell have a total flow of `0`, as when none fell or their volume is
`0`. It is `0` when the bars that rose have a total flow of `0` but those
that fell do not.

**Example:** At index 4 the 3-bar window has one rising bar with a flow of `12 * 100` and
one falling bar with `11 * 200`, so the index is
`100 - 100 / (1 + 1200 / 2200)`. No bar fell in the window at index 6, so
it is `na` there.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "volume" volume
emit "mfi" ta.mfi(close, 3)
```

```csv
time,close,volume
0,10,100
1,11,100
2,12,100
3,11,200
4,11,100
5,12,100
6,13,100
7,12,100
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  volume  mfi
0      10     100     na
1      11     100     na
2      12     100     na
3      11     200     51.11111111111111
4      11     100     35.294117647058826
5      12     100     35.294117647058826
6      13     100     na
7      12     100     67.56756756756758
```

**See also:** [`ta.rsi`](#ta.rsi), [`ta.cmo`](#ta.cmo)

entries.summary: Moving Average Convergence Divergence (MACD) of `source`: the MACD line, its signal line and the histogram.
signatures:
ta.macd(
    float source,
    simple int fastlen,
    simple int slowlen,
    simple int siglen
)

parameters.name: fastlen
parameters.description: Length of the fast average in bars, at least 1. It must be a value known when the script starts, such as a constant or an input.

parameters.name: slowlen
parameters.description: Length of the slow average in bars, at least 1. It must be a value known when the script starts, such as a constant or an input.

parameters.name: siglen
parameters.description: Length of the signal line's average in bars, at least 1. It must be a value known when the script starts, such as a constant or an input.

entries.returns: `[float, float, float]`: the MACD line, the signal line and the histogram.
entries.body:
The MACD line is the fast [`ta.ema`](#ta.ema) of `source` minus the slow one,
the signal line is the [`ta.ema`](#ta.ema) of the MACD line over the bars where
`source` is known, and the histogram is the MACD line minus the signal
line.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{macd}_t &= \mathrm{ema}(\mathit{source}, \mathit{fastlen})_t -
\mathrm{ema}(\mathit{source}, \mathit{slowlen})_t \\
\mathrm{signal}_t &= \mathrm{ema}(y, \mathit{siglen})_t, \qquad
y_t = \begin{cases} \mathrm{macd}_t & \mathit{source}_t \ne \text{na} \\
\text{na} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \\
\mathrm{histogram}_t &= \mathrm{macd}_t - \mathrm{signal}_t
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** All three are `na` before the first known value of `source` and `0`
on it, because each average starts from its first value. On a bar where
`source` is `na`, all three keep their values.

**Example:** All three are 0 on the first bar, and at index 1 the fast average is 12 and
the slow one 11.5, so the MACD line is 0.5. The close is missing at index 4,
so all three keep their values there.

```tea
[macdLine, signalLine, histogram] = ta.macd(close, 2, 3, 2)
emit "close" close
emit "macd" macdLine
emit "signal" signalLine
emit "histogram" histogram
```

```csv
time,close
0,10
1,13
2,13
3,16
4,
5,16
6,13
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  macd                  signal               histogram
0      10     0                     0                    0
1      13     0.5                   0.3333333333333333   0.16666666666666669
2      13     0.4166666666666661    0.38888888888888845  0.027777777777777624
3      16     0.7638888888888893    0.6388888888888891   0.12500000000000022
4      na     0.7638888888888893    0.6388888888888891   0.12500000000000022
5      16     0.5671296296296298    0.5910493827160496   -0.023919753086419804
6      13     -0.15470679012345556  0.09387860082304618  -0.24858539094650173
```

**See also:** [`ta.ema`](#ta.ema)

entries.summary: Directional Movement Index (DMI): the +DI and -DI lines and the Average Directional Index (ADX), each from `0` to `100`.
signatures: ta.dmi(simple int diLength, simple int adxSmoothing)

parameters.name: diLength
parameters.description: Smoothing length for +DI and -DI in bars, at least 1. It must be a value known when the script starts, such as a constant or an input.

parameters.name: adxSmoothing
parameters.description: Smoothing length for ADX in bars, at least 1. It must be a value known when the script starts, such as a constant or an input.

entries.returns: `[float, float, float]`: +DI, -DI and ADX.
entries.body:
On each bar, the rise of [`high`](#high) is the upward move and the fall of
[`low`](#low) the downward move; only the larger of the two is kept, and only
when it is positive. Each move and the true range ([`ta.tr`](#ta.tr)) are
smoothed with [`ta.rma`](#ta.rma) over `diLength` bars, and each smoothed move as
a percentage of the smoothed true range gives +DI and -DI. A bar counts
toward these three averages only when its high and low and the previous
bar's high, low and close are all known, so the first bar never counts.
ADX is `100` times the [`ta.rma`](#ta.rma), over `adxSmoothing` bars, of the
absolute difference of +DI and -DI divided by their sum.

+DI and -DI leave `0` to `100` only when a close lies above its bar's high
or below its low.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
u_t &= \mathit{high}_t - \mathit{high}_{t-1}, \qquad
d_t = \mathit{low}_{t-1} - \mathit{low}_t, \qquad
r_t = \mathrm{tr}(\text{false})_t \\
p_t &= \begin{cases} u_t & u_t > d_t \text{ and } u_t > 0 \\
0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \\
m_t &= \begin{cases} d_t & d_t > u_t \text{ and } d_t > 0 \\
0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \\
(\hat{p}_t, \hat{m}_t, \hat{r}_t) &= \begin{cases}
(p_t, m_t, r_t) & u_t, d_t, r_t \ne \text{na} \\
(\text{na}, \text{na}, \text{na}) & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases} \\
q^{+}_t &= \frac{100 \cdot \mathrm{rma}(\hat{p}, \mathit{diLength})_t}
{\mathrm{rma}(\hat{r}, \mathit{diLength})_t}, \qquad
q^{-}_t = \frac{100 \cdot \mathrm{rma}(\hat{m}, \mathit{diLength})_t}
{\mathrm{rma}(\hat{r}, \mathit{diLength})_t} \\
\mathrm{DI}^{\pm}_t &= \begin{cases} q^{\pm}_t & q^{\pm}_t \ne \text{na} \\
\mathrm{DI}^{\pm}_{t-1} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \\
x_t &= \frac{|\mathrm{DI}^{+}_t - \mathrm{DI}^{-}_t|}
{\mathrm{DI}^{+}_t + \mathrm{DI}^{-}_t},
\text{ or } 0 \text{ when both are } 0 \\
\mathrm{ADX}_t &= 100 \cdot \mathrm{rma}(x, \mathit{adxSmoothing})_t
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** +DI and -DI are `na` until `diLength` bars have counted and a
counted bar has a true range other than `0`, so always on the first
`diLength` bars. After that, on a bar that does not count or where the
smoothed true range is `0`, they keep their values and ADX still averages
them. ADX is `na` until `adxSmoothing` values of +DI and -DI are known.

**Example:** +DI and -DI start at index 3, the third bar that counts: the smoothed moves,
`4 / 3` up and `2 / 3` down, as percentages of the smoothed true range,
`11 / 3`, are about 36.36 and 18.18. The missing close at index 5 keeps
index 6 from counting, so +DI and -DI keep their values there while ADX
still moves.

```tea
[plusDI, minusDI, adx] = ta.dmi(3, 2)
emit "high" high
emit "low" low
emit "close" close
emit "+DI" plusDI
emit "-DI" minusDI
emit "ADX" adx
```

```csv
time,high,low,close
0,10,8,9
1,12,9,11
2,11,7,10
3,13,9,12
4,12,8,9
5,15,10,
6,14,9,10
7,16,11,15
```

**Output:**

```text
index  high  low  close  +DI                 -DI                 ADX
0      10    8    9      na                  na                  na
1      12    9    11     na                  na                  na
2      11    7    10     na                  na                  na
3      13    9    12     36.36363636363636   18.18181818181818   na
4      12    8    9      23.529411764705888  20.58823529411765   20
5      15    10   na     35.24590163934426   11.475409836065575  35.43859649122807
6      14    9    10     35.24590163934426   11.475409836065575  43.15789473684211
7      16    11   15     34.48275862068965   6.896551724137932   54.912280701754376
```

**See also:** [`ta.tr`](#ta.tr), [`ta.rma`](#ta.rma)

entries.summary: True range of the current bar: its high-to-low range, extended to reach the previous close.

parameters.name: handle_na
parameters.description: Result when the previous close is `na`, as on the first bar: `true` gives `high - low`; `false` gives `na`. It must be known when the script starts, such as a constant or an input.

entries.returns: `float`: the true range.
entries.body:
It measures how far price moved during the bar, counting a gap from the
previous [`close`](#close), which comes from the bar before even when the call
did not run on that bar. When that close lies between this bar's
[`low`](#low) and [`high`](#high), the true range is `high - low`. It is in
price units. [`ta.atr`](#ta.atr) averages it. Pine Script's variable `ta.tr` is
the same as `ta.tr(false)`.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{tr}_t &= \begin{cases}
\max(\mathit{high}_t - \mathit{low}_t,\ |\mathit{high}_t - c|,\
|\mathit{low}_t - c|) & c \ne \text{na} \\
\mathit{high}_t - \mathit{low}_t
& c = \text{na} \text{ and } \mathit{handle\_na} \\
\text{na} & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases} \\
\text{where}\quad c &= \mathit{close}_{t-1}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** No warm-up when `handle_na` is `true`. When it is `false`, `na` on
the first bar and on the bar after each missing close. A missing high or low
gives `na` either way.

**Example:** At index 2 the bar is above the previous close of 11, so the true range is
`15 - 11 = 4`, more than `high - low`. Index 0, and index 4 after the
missing close, have no previous close: `ta.tr(true)` gives `high - low` and
`ta.tr(false)` gives `na`.

```tea
emit "high" high
emit "low" low
emit "close" close
emit "tr(true)" ta.tr(true)
emit "tr(false)" ta.tr(false)
```

```csv
time,high,low,close
0,11,9,10
1,12,10,11
2,15,13,14
3,14,12,
4,13,11,12
5,10,8,9
```

```text
0      11    9    10     2         na
1      12    10   11     2         2
2      15    13   14     4         4
3      14    12   na     2         2
4      13    11   12     2         na
```

entries.summary: Average true range (ATR): the smoothed average of recent true ranges, a measure of volatility in price units.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Smoothing length in bars, at least 1. It must be known when the script starts, such as a constant or an input.

entries.returns: `float`: the average true range.
entries.body:
It is [`ta.rma`](#ta.rma), Wilder's moving average, of `ta.tr(true)` over
`length` bars: the simple average of the first `length` true ranges, after
which each bar moves the average `1 / length` of the way toward the new true
range ([`ta.tr`](#ta.tr)). The first bar's true range is `high - low`.

**Formula**

$$
\mathrm{atr}_t = \mathrm{rma}(\mathrm{tr}(\text{true}), \mathit{length})_t
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` until `length` true ranges that are not `na` have arrived: the
first `length - 1` bars when no high or low is missing. After that, a bar
whose true range is `na`, because its high or low is `na`, keeps the
previous value.

**Example:** Index 3 averages the first four true ranges, `(2 + 3 + 4 + 3) / 4 = 3`. The
gap at index 4 gives a true range of 7, and the ATR moves a quarter of the
way to it, `3 + (7 - 3) / 4 = 4`; the missing high at index 5 leaves it at 4.

```tea
emit "high" high
emit "low" low
emit "close" close
emit "tr" ta.tr(true)
emit "atr" ta.atr(4)
```

```csv
time,high,low,close
0,11,9,10
1,12,9,11
2,13,9,12
3,14,11,13
4,20,17,19
5,,18,19
6,20,18,19
7,25,17,24
```

**Output:**

```text
index  high  low  close  tr  atr
0      11    9    10     2   na
1      12    9    11     3   na
2      13    9    12     4   na
3      14    11   13     3   3
4      20    17   19     7   4
5      na    18   19     na  4
6      20    18   19     2   3.5
7      25    17   24     8   4.625
```

**See also:** [`ta.tr`](#ta.tr), [`ta.rma`](#ta.rma), [`ta.supertrend`](#ta.supertrend)

entries.summary: Mean absolute deviation: the average distance of the last `length` values of `source` from their mean.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of bars in the window, at least 1.

entries.returns: `float`: the mean absolute deviation, in the units of `source`.
entries.body:
The mean is the [`ta.sma`](#ta.sma) of the same window. Values that are `na` are
left out of both the mean and the average distance.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{dev}_t &= \frac{1}{|K_t|} \sum_{i \in K_t}
\left| \mathit{source}_{t-i} - \mu_t \right|,
\qquad \mu_t = \mathrm{sma}(\mathit{source}, \mathit{length})_t \\
K_t &= \{\, i : 0 \le i < \mathit{length},
\ \mathit{source}_{t-i} \ne \text{na} \,\}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` on the first `length - 1` bars, and when every value in the
window is `na`.

**Example:** At index 2 the closes 9, 12 and 15 lie 3, 0 and 3 from their mean of 12, so
the deviation is 2. The windows that hold the missing close at index 4 use
their two known values.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "sma" ta.sma(close, 3)
emit "dev" ta.dev(close, 3)
```

```csv
time,close
0,9
1,12
2,15
3,9
4,
5,9
6,12
7,15
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  sma   dev
0      9      na    na
1      12     na    na
2      15     12    2
3      9      12    2
4      na     12    3
5      9      9     0
6      12     10.5  1.5
7      15     12    2
```

**See also:** [`ta.stdev`](#ta.stdev), [`ta.variance`](#ta.variance), [`ta.cci`](#ta.cci)

entries.summary: Variance: how widely the last `length` values of `source` spread around their mean, in squared units.
signatures: ta.variance(float source, int length, bool biased = true)

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of bars in the window, at least 1.

parameters.name: biased
parameters.description: `true` (the default) divides by the number of known values, giving the population variance; `false` divides by one less, giving the sample variance.

entries.returns: `float`: the variance, in the units of `source` squared.
entries.body:
Values that are `na` are left out, so the mean is the average of the known
values. Known values that are all equal give exactly `0`, even when they are
decimals.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{variance}_t &= \frac{1}{d_t} \sum_{i \in K_t}
\left( \mathit{source}_{t-i} - \mu_t \right)^2,
\qquad \mu_t = \frac{1}{|K_t|} \sum_{i \in K_t} \mathit{source}_{t-i} \\
d_t &= \begin{cases}
|K_t| & \text{if } \mathit{biased} \\
|K_t| - 1 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases} \\
K_t &= \{\, i : 0 \le i < \mathit{length},
\ \mathit{source}_{t-i} \ne \text{na} \,\}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` on the first `length - 1` bars, and when every value in the
window is `na`. With `biased` set to `false`, also `na` when only one value
in the window is known.

**Example:** At index 2 the closes 10, 13 and 16 lie 3, 0 and 3 from their mean, so the
squared distances sum to 18: divided by 3 it is 6, and by 2 it is 9. The
windows that hold the missing close at index 4 have two known values, so
they divide by 2 and 1.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "population" ta.variance(close, 3)
emit "sample" ta.variance(close, 3, biased = false)
```

```csv
time,close
0,10
1,13
2,16
3,13
4,
5,15
6,12
7,12
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  population  sample
0      10     na          na
1      13     na          na
2      16     6           9
3      13     2           3
4      na     2.25        4.5
5      15     1           2
6      12     2.25        4.5
7      12     2           3
```

**See also:** [`ta.stdev`](#ta.stdev), [`ta.dev`](#ta.dev)

entries.summary: Standard deviation: how widely the last `length` values of `source` spread around their mean.
signatures: ta.stdev(float source, int length, bool biased = true)

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of bars in the window, at least 1.

parameters.name: biased
parameters.description: `true` (the default) uses the population variance, which divides by the number of known values; `false` uses the sample variance, which divides by one less.

entries.returns: `float`: the standard deviation, in the units of `source`.
entries.body:
It is the square root of [`ta.variance`](#ta.variance) with the same arguments, so it
is in the units of `source`. Values that are `na` are left out, and known
values that are all equal give exactly `0`, even when they are decimals.

**Formula**

$$
\mathrm{stdev}_t =
\sqrt{\mathrm{variance}(\mathit{source}, \mathit{length}, \mathit{biased})_t}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` on the first `length - 1` bars, and when every value in the
window is `na`. With `biased` set to `false`, also `na` when only one value
in the window is known.

**Example:** At indexes 3 to 5 each 4-bar window holds two 10s and two 12s, each 1 from
their mean of 11, so the standard deviation is 1. The windows that hold the
18 at index 6 give 3.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "stdev" ta.stdev(close, 4)
```

```csv
time,close
0,10
1,12
2,10
3,12
4,10
5,12
6,18
7,12
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  stdev
0      10     na
1      12     na
2      10     na
3      12     1
4      10     1
5      12     1
6      18     3
7      12     3
```

**See also:** [`ta.variance`](#ta.variance), [`ta.bb`](#ta.bb), [`ta.dev`](#ta.dev)

entries.summary: Range of the last `length` values of `source`: the highest minus the lowest.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of bars in the window, at least 1.

entries.returns: `float`: the highest value in the window minus the lowest.
entries.body:
It is [`ta.highest`](#ta.highest) minus [`ta.lowest`](#ta.lowest) with the same arguments.
Values that are `na` are left out of both.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{range}_t &= \max_{i \in K_t} \mathit{source}_{t-i}
- \min_{i \in K_t} \mathit{source}_{t-i} \\
K_t &= \{\, i : 0 \le i < \mathit{length},
\ \mathit{source}_{t-i} \ne \text{na} \,\}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` on the first `length - 1` bars, and when every value in the
window is `na`.

**Example:** At index 3 the closes 12, 11 and 15 give 15 minus 11, which is 4. The
windows that hold the missing close at index 4 use their two known values.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "range" ta.range(close, 3)
```

```csv
time,close
0,10
1,12
2,11
3,15
4,
5,13
6,9
7,10
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  range
0      10     na
1      12     na
2      11     2
3      15     4
4      na     4
5      13     2
6      9      4
7      10     4
```

**Pine Script:** Pine's manual gives an `int` result for an `int` source; Tea's
result is always `float`.

**See also:** [`ta.highest`](#ta.highest), [`ta.lowest`](#ta.lowest)

entries.summary: Bollinger Bands: the simple moving average of `series`, with bands `mult` standard deviations above and below it.
signatures: ta.bb(float series, int length, simple float mult)

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of bars in the window, at least 1.

parameters.name: mult
parameters.description: Band distance in standard deviations, such as `2`. It must be known when the script starts, such as a constant or an input.

entries.returns: `[float, float, float]`: the middle band, the upper band and the lower band.
entries.body:
The middle band is [`ta.sma`](#ta.sma) and the distance is `mult` times the
population standard deviation, [`ta.stdev`](#ta.stdev) with `biased` `true`, both
over the last `length` values. [`ta.bbw`](#ta.bbw) gives the distance between
the bands relative to the middle band.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathit{middle}_t &= \mathrm{sma}(\mathit{series}, \mathit{length})_t \\
\mathit{upper}_t &= \mathit{middle}_t
  + \mathit{mult} \cdot \mathrm{stdev}(\mathit{series}, \mathit{length})_t \\
\mathit{lower}_t &= \mathit{middle}_t
  - \mathit{mult} \cdot \mathrm{stdev}(\mathit{series}, \mathit{length})_t
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** All three are `na` on the first `length - 1` bars, and when every
value in the window is `na`. Other `na` values are left out of the window.

**Example:** At index 3 the window holds 10, 12, 10 and 12: the middle band is 11 and
the standard deviation 1, so the bands are 13 and 9. The close is missing
at index 4, so the windows that hold it use their other three values.

```tea
[middle, upper, lower] = ta.bb(close, 4, 2)
emit "close" close
emit "middle" middle
emit "upper" upper
emit "lower" lower
```

```csv
time,close
0,10
1,12
2,10
3,12
4,
5,12
6,14
7,12
8,14
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  middle              upper               lower
0      10     na                  na                  na
1      12     na                  na                  na
2      10     na                  na                  na
3      12     11                  13                  9
4      na     11.333333333333334  13.218951416497461  9.447715250169207
5      12     11.333333333333334  13.218951416497461  9.447715250169207
6      14     12.666666666666666  14.552284749830793  10.781048583502539
7      12     12.666666666666666  14.552284749830793  10.781048583502539
8      14     13                  15                  11
```

**See also:** [`ta.bbw`](#ta.bbw), [`ta.kc`](#ta.kc), [`ta.stdev`](#ta.stdev)

entries.summary: Bollinger Band width: the distance between the upper and lower [`ta.bb`](#ta.bb) bands as a percentage of the middle band.
signatures: ta.bbw(float series, int length, simple float mult)

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of bars in the window, at least 1.

parameters.name: mult
parameters.description: Band distance in standard deviations, such as `2`. It must be known when the script starts, such as a constant or an input.

entries.returns: `float`: the width in percent of the middle band.
entries.body:
It is small when the values in the window are close together. Unlike
[`ta.kcw`](#ta.kcw), it is multiplied by `100`.

**Formula**

$$
\mathrm{bbw}_t = 100 \cdot \frac{2 \cdot \mathit{mult}
  \cdot \mathrm{stdev}(\mathit{series}, \mathit{length})_t}
  {\mathrm{sma}(\mathit{series}, \mathit{length})_t}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` on the first `length - 1` bars, when every value in the window
is `na`, and when the middle band is `0`. Other `na` values are left out of
the window.

**Example:** While the closes swing between 19 and 21, the middle band is 20 and the
standard deviation 1, so the width is `100 * 2 * 2 * 1 / 20 = 20`. The jump
to 25 at index 6 widens it.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "bbw" ta.bbw(close, 4, 2)
```

```csv
time,close
0,19
1,21
2,19
3,21
4,19
5,21
6,25
7,25
```

**Output:**

