```text
0      19     na
1      21     na
2      19     na
3      21     20
4      19     20
5      21     20
6      25     40.54789714921557
7      25     46.188021535170066
```

**See also:** [`ta.bb`](#ta.bb), [`ta.kcw`](#ta.kcw)

entries.summary: Keltner Channels: the exponential moving average of `series`, with bands `mult` average ranges above and below it.
signatures:
ta.kc(
    float series,
    simple int length,
    simple float mult,
    simple bool useTrueRange = true
)

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Smoothing length in bars for both averages, at least 1. It must be known when the script starts, such as a constant or an input.

parameters.name: mult
parameters.description: Band distance in average ranges, such as `2`. It must be known when the script starts, such as a constant or an input.

parameters.name: useTrueRange
parameters.description: `true`, the default, measures each bar's range with `ta.tr(false)`; `false` uses `high - low`. It must be known when the script starts, such as a constant or an input.

entries.returns: `[float, float, float]`: the middle line, the upper band and the lower band.
entries.body:
The middle line is [`ta.ema`](#ta.ema) of `series`. The distance is `mult` times
the [`ta.ema`](#ta.ema), over the same `length`, of each bar's range: its true
range ([`ta.tr`](#ta.tr)), or `high - low` when `useTrueRange` is `false`. This
average range is an exponential average, not [`ta.atr`](#ta.atr).

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathit{middle}_t &= \mathrm{ema}(\mathit{series}, \mathit{length})_t \\
\mathit{upper}_t &= \mathit{middle}_t
  + \mathit{mult} \cdot \mathrm{ema}(r, \mathit{length})_t \\
\mathit{lower}_t &= \mathit{middle}_t
  - \mathit{mult} \cdot \mathrm{ema}(r, \mathit{length})_t \\
r_t &= \begin{cases}
  \mathrm{tr}(\text{false})_t & \mathit{useTrueRange} \\
  \mathit{high}_t - \mathit{low}_t & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** The middle line is `na` until the first `series` value that is not
`na`. The bands are also `na` until the first range that is not `na`. The
range is `na` when the high or low is `na`, and with `useTrueRange` also
when the previous close is `na`, as on the first bar. After that, a bar
where `series` is `na` keeps the middle line, and a bar where the range is
`na` keeps the average range.

**Example:** The middle line starts at the first close and moves halfway to each new
close. The bands start at index 1, the first bar with a previous close: its
true range is `13 - 10 = 3`, so they sit `2 * 3 = 6` from the middle.

```tea
[middle, upper, lower] = ta.kc(close, 3, 2)
emit "high" high
emit "low" low
emit "close" close
emit "middle" middle
emit "upper" upper
emit "lower" lower
```

```csv
time,high,low,close
0,11,9,10
1,13,11,12
2,12,10,11
3,14,12,13
4,14,12,13
5,16,14,15
```

**Output:**

```text
index  high  low  close  middle  upper   lower
0      11    9    10     10      na      na
1      13    11   12     11      17      5
2      12    10   11     11      16      6
3      14    12   13     12      17.5    6.5
4      14    12   13     12.5    17.25   7.75
5      16    14   15     13.75   19.125  8.375
```

**See also:** [`ta.kcw`](#ta.kcw), [`ta.bb`](#ta.bb), [`ta.atr`](#ta.atr)

entries.summary: Keltner Channel width: the distance between the upper and lower [`ta.kc`](#ta.kc) bands as a fraction of the middle line.
signatures:
ta.kcw(
    float series,
    simple int length,
    simple float mult,
    simple bool useTrueRange = true
)

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Smoothing length in bars for both averages, at least 1. It must be known when the script starts, such as a constant or an input.

parameters.name: mult
parameters.description: Band distance in average ranges, such as `2`. It must be known when the script starts, such as a constant or an input.

parameters.name: useTrueRange
parameters.description: `true`, the default, measures each bar's range with `ta.tr(false)`; `false` uses `high - low`. It must be known when the script starts, such as a constant or an input.

entries.returns: `float`: the width as a fraction of the middle line.
entries.body:
Unlike [`ta.bbw`](#ta.bbw), it is not multiplied by `100`.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{kcw}_t &= \frac{\mathit{upper}_t - \mathit{lower}_t}{\mathit{middle}_t} \\
\text{where}\quad [\mathit{middle}, \mathit{upper}, \mathit{lower}]
&= \mathrm{kc}(\mathit{series}, \mathit{length}, \mathit{mult},
\mathit{useTrueRange})
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` where [`ta.kc`](#ta.kc) gives `na` bands, as on the first bar when
`useTrueRange` is `true`, and where the middle line is `0`.

**Example:** At index 1 the bands are 17 and 5 around a middle line of 11, so the width
is `12 / 11`. With `useTrueRange` `false` the first bar has a width, and the
widths are smaller because `high - low` leaves out the gaps from the
previous close.

```tea
emit "high" high
emit "low" low
emit "close" close
emit "kcw" ta.kcw(close, 3, 2)
emit "kcwHighLow" ta.kcw(close, 3, 2, false)
```

```csv
0,11,9,10
1,13,11,12
2,12,10,11
3,14,12,13
4,14,12,13
5,16,14,15
```

**Output:**

```text
0      11    9    10     na                  0.8
1      13    11   12     1.0909090909090908  0.7272727272727273
2      12    10   11     0.9090909090909091  0.7272727272727273
3      14    12   13     0.9166666666666666  0.6666666666666666
4      14    12   13     0.76                0.64
```

entries.summary: Supertrend: a trailing line below price in an uptrend and above it in a downtrend, with the trend direction.

parameters.name: factor
parameters.description: Band distance in average true ranges, such as `3`.

parameters.name: atrPeriod
parameters.description: Length of the [`ta.atr`](#ta.atr), at least 1. It must be known when the script starts, such as a constant or an input.

entries.returns: `[float, int]`: the line, then the direction: `-1` in an uptrend and `1` in a downtrend.
entries.body:
Two bands sit `factor` times [`ta.atr`](#ta.atr) above and below [`hl2`](#hl2). The
lower band never falls unless the previous [`close`](#close) was below it, and
the upper band never rises unless the previous close was above it. In a
downtrend the line is the upper band, and the trend turns up when `close`
rises above it; in an uptrend the line is the lower band, and the trend
turns down when `close` falls below it.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
A_t &= \mathrm{atr}(\mathit{atrPeriod})_t, \quad
  \hat{U}_t = \mathit{hl2}_t + \mathit{factor} \cdot A_t, \quad
  \hat{L}_t = \mathit{hl2}_t - \mathit{factor} \cdot A_t \\
U_t &= \begin{cases}
  \hat{U}_t & \hat{U}_t < U'_t \text{ or } \mathit{close}_{t-1} > U'_t \\
  U'_t & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases} \qquad U'_t = \mathrm{nz}(U_{t-1}) \\
L_t &= \begin{cases}
  \hat{L}_t & \hat{L}_t > L'_t \text{ or } \mathit{close}_{t-1} < L'_t \\
  L'_t & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases} \qquad L'_t = \mathrm{nz}(L_{t-1}) \\
\mathit{direction}_t &= \begin{cases}
  1 & \text{if } A_{t-1} = \text{na} \\
  -1 \text{ if } \mathit{close}_t > U_t \text{, else } 1
    & \text{else if } \mathit{line}_{t-1} = U'_t \\
  1 \text{ if } \mathit{close}_t < L_t \text{, else } -1 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases} \\
\mathit{line}_t &= \begin{cases}
  L_t & \mathit{direction}_t = -1 \\
  U_t & \mathit{direction}_t = 1
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `direction` is `1` up to and including the bar where the ATR gets
its first value: the first `atrPeriod` bars when no high or low is missing.
With prices above `0`, `line` is `0` on the first bar and `na` on the later
bars where the ATR is `na`; a missing close before the ATR's first value
makes `line` `0` on the next bar. After that, a bar whose `close` is `na`
keeps the direction. On a bar whose [`hl2`](#hl2) is `na`, a band keeps its
previous value, or is `na` if the previous close was beyond it.

**Example:** After the placeholder `0` at index 0, the line is the upper band,
`hl2 + atr`: `10.5 + 2.5 = 13`, then 12.25, where it stays because that
band does not rise. At index 5 the close of 14 is above it, so `direction`
turns to `-1` and the line drops to the lower band, 8.

```tea
[line, direction] = ta.supertrend(1, 2)
emit "high" high
emit "low" low
emit "close" close
emit "atr" ta.atr(2)
emit "line" line
emit "direction" direction
```

```csv
time,high,low,close
0,10,8,9
1,12,9,11
2,11,7,10
3,13,9,12
4,12,8,9
5,15,10,14
6,14,9,10
7,16,11,15
```

**Output:**

```text
index  high  low  close  atr        line       direction
0      10    8    9      na         0          1
1      12    9    11     2.5        13         1
2      11    7    10     3.25       12.25      1
3      13    9    12     3.625      12.25      1
4      12    8    9      3.8125     12.25      1
5      15    10   14     4.90625    8          -1
6      14    9    10     4.953125   8          -1
7      16    11   15     5.4765625  8.0234375  -1
```

**Pine Script:** Pine's manual gives `direction` as `float`; Tea returns it as an
`int`.

**See also:** [`ta.atr`](#ta.atr), [`ta.sar`](#ta.sar)

entries.summary: Parabolic SAR (stop and reverse): a trailing stop level that follows the trend and speeds up as the trend makes new extremes.
signatures: ta.sar(simple float start, simple float inc, simple float max)

parameters.name: start
parameters.description: Initial acceleration factor, such as `0.02`. It must be known when the script starts, such as a constant or an input.

parameters.name: inc
parameters.description: Increase of the acceleration factor at each new extreme point, such as `0.02`. It must be known when the script starts, such as a constant or an input.

parameters.name: max
parameters.description: Largest acceleration factor, such as `0.2`. It must be known when the script starts, such as a constant or an input.

entries.returns: `float`: the stop level.
entries.body:
A bar counts when the call runs on it and its [`high`](#high), [`low`](#low) and
[`close`](#close) are all known. On a bar with a missing price the level holds.
Below, "the previous bar" means the latest earlier bar that counts.

The trend starts on the second bar that counts. If the close rose from the
previous bar, it is an uptrend: the level starts at the previous bar's low
and the extreme point at this bar's high. Otherwise it is a downtrend: the
level starts at the previous bar's high and the extreme point at this bar's
low. The acceleration factor starts at `start`. Then each bar that counts,
from that one on, takes these steps:

1. The level moves toward the extreme point by the acceleration factor
   times the distance between them.
2. In an uptrend, if that level is above the bar's low, the trend turns
   down: the level jumps to the higher of the extreme point and the bar's
   high, the extreme point becomes the bar's low, and the factor returns to
   `start`. A downtrend turns up the same way when the level is below the
   bar's high.
3. Otherwise, a high above the extreme point in an uptrend, or a low below
   it in a downtrend, becomes the new extreme point and raises the factor by
   `inc`, up to `max`.
4. If the trend is now up, the level is lowered to the lowest low of the
   previous two bars if it is above it; if it is now down, the level is
   raised to their highest high if it is below it. On the bar where the
   trend starts, there is only one previous bar.

Step 2 compares the bar with the level from step 1, before step 4. That
level is not the one plotted on the previous bar: in an uptrend it is at or
above it, so a low below the previous plotted level always turns the trend,
a low a little above it can too, and a low equal to the step 1 level does
not. The same holds for highs in a downtrend. On a bar that does not turn,
the plotted level is the step 1 level, or lower after step 4 (higher in a
downtrend).

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
S^{*}_t &= S_p + a_p \cdot (E_p - S_p) \\[4pt]
&\text{in an uptrend:} \\
S_t &= \begin{cases}
  \max(E_p, \mathit{high}_t, \mathit{high}_p, \mathit{high}_q)
    & S^{*}_t > \mathit{low}_t \text{ (turns down)} \\
  \min(S^{*}_t, \mathit{low}_p, \mathit{low}_q) & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases} \\
(E_t, a_t) &= \begin{cases}
  (\mathit{low}_t, \mathit{start}) & S^{*}_t > \mathit{low}_t \\
  (\mathit{high}_t, \min(a_p + \mathit{inc}, \mathit{max}))
    & \mathit{high}_t > E_p \\
  (E_p, a_p) & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases} \\[4pt]
&\text{in a downtrend:} \\
S_t &= \begin{cases}
  \min(E_p, \mathit{low}_t, \mathit{low}_p, \mathit{low}_q)
    & S^{*}_t < \mathit{high}_t \text{ (turns up)} \\
  \max(S^{*}_t, \mathit{high}_p, \mathit{high}_q) & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases} \\
(E_t, a_t) &= \begin{cases}
  (\mathit{high}_t, \mathit{start}) & S^{*}_t < \mathit{high}_t \\
  (\mathit{low}_t, \min(a_p + \mathit{inc}, \mathit{max}))
    & \mathit{low}_t < E_p \\
  (E_p, a_p) & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases} \\[4pt]
&\text{where the trend starts, without the terms for bar } q\text{:} \\
(S_p, E_p, a_p) &= \begin{cases}
  (\mathit{low}_p, \mathit{high}_t, \mathit{start}) \text{, uptrend}
    & \mathit{close}_t > \mathit{close}_p \\
  (\mathit{high}_p, \mathit{low}_t, \mathit{start}) \text{, downtrend}
    & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases} \\[4pt]
&\text{where } p, q \text{ are the latest and second-latest earlier bars
  that count,} \\
&\text{and } S_t = S_{t-1} \text{ on a bar with a missing high, low or close}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` until the second bar on which the call runs with a known high,
low and close: only on the first bar for a call that runs on every bar with
no missing price. After that it is never `na`: a bar with a missing high,
low or close keeps the previous level. An `na` `start`, `inc` or `max`
gives `na` on every bar.

**Example:** The close rises at index 1, so the trend starts up from the previous low,
8; the level then climbs, holding at 8.8 at index 4, where the low is
missing. At index 6 the low of 9 is below the level, so the trend turns
down and the level jumps to 14, the highest high of the uptrend.

```tea
emit "high" high
emit "low" low
emit "close" close
emit "sar" ta.sar(0.1, 0.1, 0.2)
```

```csv
time,high,low,close
0,10,8,9
1,11,9,10.5
2,12,10,11.5
3,13,11,12.5
4,13,,12.8
5,14,12,13.5
6,13,9,9.5
7,12,8,8.5
8,11,7,7.5
9,10,6,6.5
```

**Output:**

```text
index  high  low  close  sar
0      10    8    9      na
1      11    9    10.5   8
2      12    10   11.5   8
3      13    11   12.5   8.8
4      13    na   12.8   8.8
5      14    12   13.5   9.64
6      13    9    9.5    14
7      12    8    8.5    14
8      11    7    7.5    13
9      10    6    6.5    12
```

**Pine Script:** The reference code in Pine's manual starts the trend on the bar where
`bar_index` is `1` and does not skip bars with a missing price. Tea starts
on the second bar on which the call runs with a known high, low and close,
and skips the bars without them; when every price is known and the call
runs on every bar, the levels are the same.

**See also:** [`ta.supertrend`](#ta.supertrend)

entries.summary: Crossover: `true` on the bar where `source1` moves from at or below `source2` to above it.

parameters.name: source1
parameters.description: Series that crosses, such as a fast moving average.

parameters.name: source2
parameters.description: Series or fixed level that `source1` crosses.

entries.returns: `bool`: `true` on the bar of the cross, otherwise `false`.
entries.body:
Equality counts as below on the previous bar but not as above on the
current one, so `source1` touching `source2` and moving back above it is a
cross.

**Formula**

$$
\mathrm{crossover}_t =
(\mathit{source1}_t > \mathit{source2}_t)
\land
(\mathit{source1}_{t-1} \le \mathit{source2}_{t-1})
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `false` on the first bar. A comparison with `na` is `false`, so the
result is also `false` on a bar where `source1` or `source2` is `na` and on
the bar after it: a cross that spans an `na` bar is not reported.

**Example:** The close crosses above 50 at indices 2 and 5; at index 5 it moves back
above after touching 50 at index 4. The rise from 48 to 53 is not reported,
because the close between them, at index 7, is missing.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "crossover" ta.crossover(close, 50)
```

```csv
time,close
0,49
1,50
2,51
3,52
4,50
5,51
6,48
7,
8,53
9,54
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  crossover
0      49     false
1      50     false
2      51     true
3      52     false
4      50     false
5      51     true
6      48     false
7      na     false
8      53     false
9      54     false
```

**See also:** [`ta.crossunder`](#ta.crossunder), [`ta.cross`](#ta.cross)

entries.summary: Crossunder: `true` on the bar where `source1` moves from at or above `source2` to below it.

parameters.name: source1
parameters.description: Series that crosses, such as a fast moving average.

parameters.name: source2
parameters.description: Series or fixed level that `source1` crosses.

entries.returns: `bool`: `true` on the bar of the cross, otherwise `false`.
entries.body:
Equality counts as above on the previous bar but not as below on the
current one, so `source1` touching `source2` and moving back below it is a
cross.

**Formula**

$$
\mathrm{crossunder}_t =
(\mathit{source1}_t < \mathit{source2}_t)
\land
(\mathit{source1}_{t-1} \ge \mathit{source2}_{t-1})
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `false` on the first bar. A comparison with `na` is `false`, so the
result is also `false` on a bar where `source1` or `source2` is `na` and on
the bar after it: a cross that spans an `na` bar is not reported.

**Example:** The close crosses below 50 at indices 2 and 5; at index 5 it moves back
below after touching 50 at index 4. The fall from 52 to 47 is not reported,
because the close between them, at index 7, is missing.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "crossunder" ta.crossunder(close, 50)
```

```csv
time,close
0,51
1,50
2,49
3,48
4,50
5,49
6,52
7,
8,47
9,46
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  crossunder
0      51     false
1      50     false
2      49     true
3      48     false
4      50     false
5      49     true
6      52     false
7      na     false
8      47     false
9      46     false
```

**See also:** [`ta.crossover`](#ta.crossover), [`ta.cross`](#ta.cross)

entries.summary: Cross: `true` on the bar where `source1` crosses `source2` in either direction.

parameters.name: source1
parameters.description: Series that crosses, such as a fast moving average.

parameters.name: source2
parameters.description: Series or fixed level that `source1` crosses.

entries.returns: `bool`: `true` on the bar of the cross, otherwise `false`.
entries.body:
It is `true` when [`ta.crossover`](#ta.crossover) or [`ta.crossunder`](#ta.crossunder) is.
Equality on the previous bar counts as either side, so `source1` touching
`source2` and moving back to the side it came from is also a cross.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{cross}_t ={}
& (\mathit{source1}_t > \mathit{source2}_t
\land \mathit{source1}_{t-1} \le \mathit{source2}_{t-1}) \\
\lor{}
& (\mathit{source1}_t < \mathit{source2}_t
\land \mathit{source1}_{t-1} \ge \mathit{source2}_{t-1})
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `false` on the first bar. A comparison with `na` is `false`, so the
result is also `false` on a bar where `source1` or `source2` is `na` and on
the bar after it: a cross that spans an `na` bar is not reported.

**Example:** `true` at indices 1, 2 and 7, where the close moves across 50, and at index
4, where it moves back below after touching 50 at index 3. The missing close
at index 5 hides the rise from 49 to 52.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "cross" ta.cross(close, 50)
```

```csv
time,close
0,49
1,51
2,49
3,50
4,49
5,
6,52
7,48
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  cross
0      49     false
1      51     true
2      49     true
3      50     false
4      49     true
5      na     false
6      52     false
7      48     true
```

**See also:** [`ta.crossover`](#ta.crossover), [`ta.crossunder`](#ta.crossunder)

entries.summary: Rising: `true` when `source` is greater than each of its previous `length` values.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of previous bars to compare with, at least 1.

entries.returns: `bool`: `true` when `source` is greater than every known previous value in the window, otherwise `false`.
entries.body:
Each previous value is compared with the current one, so the values in
between need not rise bar by bar. Previous values that are `na` are left
out.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{rising}_t &= (\mathit{source}_t \ne \text{na})
\land (K_t \ne \varnothing) \\
&\quad \land \Big(\mathit{source}_t > \max_{i \in K_t} \mathit{source}_{t-i}\Big) \\
\text{where}\quad K_t &= \{\, i : 1 \le i \le \mathit{length},
\ \mathit{source}_{t-i} \ne \text{na} \,\}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `false` on the first `length` bars. After that, `false` when
`source` is `na` or every previous value in the window is `na`.

**Example:** Index 3 is `true` although the close fell at index 2, while index 4 is
`false` because 13 is not greater than 13. At index 6 the missing close is
left out, so 14 is compared with 13 only.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "rising" ta.rising(close, 2)
```

```csv
time,close
0,10
1,12
2,11
3,13
4,13
5,
6,14
7,15
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  rising
0      10     false
1      12     false
2      11     false
3      13     true
4      13     false
5      na     false
6      14     true
7      15     true
```

**See also:** [`ta.falling`](#ta.falling), [`ta.highest`](#ta.highest)

entries.summary: Falling: `true` when `source` is less than each of its previous `length` values.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of previous bars to compare with, at least 1.

entries.returns: `bool`: `true` when `source` is less than every known previous value in the window, otherwise `false`.
entries.body:
Each previous value is compared with the current one, so the values in
between need not fall bar by bar. Previous values that are `na` are left
out.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{falling}_t &= (\mathit{source}_t \ne \text{na})
\land (K_t \ne \varnothing) \\
&\quad \land \Big(\mathit{source}_t < \min_{i \in K_t} \mathit{source}_{t-i}\Big) \\
\text{where}\quad K_t &= \{\, i : 1 \le i \le \mathit{length},
\ \mathit{source}_{t-i} \ne \text{na} \,\}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `false` on the first `length` bars. After that, `false` when
`source` is `na` or every previous value in the window is `na`.

**Example:** Index 3 is `true` although the close rose at index 2, while index 4 is
`false` because 7 is not less than 7. At index 6 the missing close is left
out, so 6 is compared with 7 only.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "falling" ta.falling(close, 2)
```

```csv
time,close
0,10
1,8
2,9
3,7
4,7
5,
6,6
7,5
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  falling
0      10     false
1      8      false
2      9      false
3      7      true
4      7      false
5      na     false
6      6      true
7      5      true
```

**See also:** [`ta.rising`](#ta.rising), [`ta.lowest`](#ta.lowest)

entries.summary: Bars since a condition: the number of bars since `condition` was last `true`.

parameters.name: condition
parameters.description: Condition to track, a `bool` such as `close > open`.

entries.returns: `int`: `0` on a bar where `condition` is `true`, otherwise one more than on the previous bar.
entries.body:
**Formula**

$$
\mathrm{barssince}_t =
\begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } \mathit{condition}_t \\
\mathrm{barssince}_{t-1} + 1 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` until the first bar where `condition` is `true`, and never `na`
after it.

**Example:** It is `na` until the close first rises above 50 at index 2. The missing
close at index 5 is not above 50, so the count goes on.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "barssince" ta.barssince(close > 50)
```

```csv
time,close
0,48
1,49
2,52
3,51
4,47
5,
6,46
7,53
8,49
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  barssince
0      48     na
1      49     na
2      52     0
3      51     0
4      47     1
5      na     2
6      46     3
7      53     0
8      49     1
```

**See also:** [`ta.crossover`](#ta.crossover), [`ta.highestbars`](#ta.highestbars)

entries.summary: Highest value: the maximum of the last `length` values of `source`.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of bars in the window, at least 1.

entries.returns: `float`: the highest value in the window.
entries.body:
The window includes the current bar. Values that are `na` are left out. To
compare with earlier bars only, read the result's history:

```tea
upper = ta.highest(high, 20)
emit "breakout" close > upper[1]
```

**Formula**

$$
\mathrm{highest}_t = \max_{i \in K_t} \mathit{source}_{t-i}
\quad\text{where}\quad
K_t = \{\, i : 0 \le i < \mathit{length},
\ \mathit{source}_{t-i} \ne \text{na} \,\}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` on the first `length - 1` bars, and when every value in the
window is `na`.

**Example:** The highest close of the last 3 bars. The first two bars are `na`, and the
missing close at index 4 is left out of the windows that hold it.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "highest" ta.highest(close, 3)
```

```csv
time,close
0,10
1,12
2,11
3,9
4,
5,8
6,13
7,10
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  highest
0      10     na
1      12     na
2      11     12
3      9      12
4      na     11
5      8      9
6      13     13
7      10     13
```

**Pine Script:** Pine also has a one-argument form, `ta.highest(length)`, that
searches `high`. Tea always takes `source`.

**See also:** [`ta.lowest`](#ta.lowest), [`ta.highestbars`](#ta.highestbars)

entries.summary: Lowest value: the minimum of the last `length` values of `source`.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of bars in the window, at least 1.

entries.returns: `float`: the lowest value in the window.
entries.body:
The window includes the current bar. Values that are `na` are left out.

**Formula**

$$
\mathrm{lowest}_t = \min_{i \in K_t} \mathit{source}_{t-i}
\quad\text{where}\quad
K_t = \{\, i : 0 \le i < \mathit{length},
\ \mathit{source}_{t-i} \ne \text{na} \,\}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` on the first `length - 1` bars, and when every value in the
window is `na`.

**Example:** The lowest close of the last 3 bars. The first two bars are `na`, and the
missing close at index 4 is left out of the windows that hold it.

```tea

emit "lowest" ta.lowest(close, 3)
```

```csv

1,8
2,9
3,11
4,
5,12
6,7
7,10
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  lowest
0      10     na
1      8      na
2      9      8
3      11     8
4      na     9
5      12     11
```

entries.summary: Offset to the highest value: `0` when the maximum of the last `length` values of `source` is on the current bar, `-1` when it is on the previous bar, and so on.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of bars in the window, at least 1.

entries.returns: `int`: the offset, from `1 - length` to `0`.
entries.body:
`bar_index + ta.highestbars(source, length)` is the bar index of the
highest value. Ties go to the most recent bar. Values that are `na` are left
out.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{highestbars}_t &= -\min \Big\{\, i \in K_t :
\mathit{source}_{t-i} = \max_{j \in K_t} \mathit{source}_{t-j} \,\Big\} \\
\text{where}\quad K_t &= \{\, i : 0 \le i < \mathit{length},
\ \mathit{source}_{t-i} \ne \text{na} \,\}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` on the first `length - 1` bars, and when every value in the
window is `na`.

**Example:** At index 3 the close of 12 ties with the one two bars back, and the most
recent wins. At index 5 the highest close is two bars back; the missing
close at index 4 is left out.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "highestbars" ta.highestbars(close, 3)
```

```csv
time,close
0,10
1,12
2,11
3,12
4,
5,9
6,13
7,13
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  highestbars
0      10     na
1      12     na
2      11     -1
3      12     0
4      na     -1
5      9      -2
6      13     0
7      13     0
```

**Pine Script:** Pine also has a one-argument form, `ta.highestbars(length)`, that
searches `high`. Tea always takes `source`.

**See also:** [`ta.highest`](#ta.highest), [`ta.lowestbars`](#ta.lowestbars)

entries.summary: Pivot high: the value `rightbars` bars back when it is higher than the `leftbars` values before it and the `rightbars` values after it, otherwise `na`.
signatures: ta.pivothigh(float source, int leftbars, int rightbars)

parameters.name: leftbars
parameters.description: Number of bars before the pivot that must be lower, at least 0.

parameters.name: rightbars
parameters.description: Number of bars after the pivot that must be lower, at least 0.

entries.returns: `float`: the pivot's value on the bar that reports it, otherwise `na`.
entries.body:
The pivot must be strictly higher than each of these `leftbars + rightbars`
neighbors: a tie with any of them is not a pivot. Neighbors that are `na`
are left out, but at least one must be known, unless `leftbars` and
`rightbars` are both `0`. A pivot is reported `rightbars` bars after its own
bar, so `bar_index - rightbars` is the bar index of the pivot.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{pivothigh}_t &=
\begin{cases}
p_t & \text{if } (J_t \ne \varnothing \lor n = 0)
\text{ and } \mathit{source}_{t-i} < p_t \text{ for every } i \in J_t \\
\text{na} & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases} \\
p_t &= \mathit{source}_{t-\mathit{rightbars}}, \qquad
n = \mathit{leftbars} + \mathit{rightbars} \\
J_t &= \{\, i : 0 \le i \le n,\ i \ne \mathit{rightbars},
\ \mathit{source}_{t-i} \ne \text{na} \,\}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` on the first `leftbars + rightbars` bars, so a value with fewer
than `leftbars` bars before it is never a pivot. After that, `na` on a bar
where the value `rightbars` bars back is `na`, or where that value has
neighbors and all of them are `na`.

**Example:** Two bars on each side, so the first four bars are `na` and the 13 at index
0, with no bars before it, is never a pivot. Index 5 reports the 12 at index
3, leaving out the missing high at index 4, and index 11 reports the 15 at
index 9; the equal highs at indices 6 and 7 are not pivots.

```tea
emit "high" high
emit "pivothigh" ta.pivothigh(high, 2, 2)
```

```csv
time,high
0,13
1,11
2,10
3,12
4,
5,11
6,14
7,14
8,10
9,15
10,9
11,8
```

**Output:**

```text
index  high  pivothigh
0      13    na
1      11    na
2      10    na
3      12    na
4      na    na
5      11    12
6      14    na
7      14    na
8      10    na
9      15    na
10     9     na
11     8     15
```

**Pine Script:** Pine also has a two-argument form without `source`,
`ta.pivothigh(leftbars, rightbars)`; Tea always takes `source`. `leftbars`
and `rightbars` must be `int`, where Pine also accepts a `float`.

**See also:** [`ta.pivotlow`](#ta.pivotlow), [`ta.highest`](#ta.highest)

entries.summary: Pivot low: the value `rightbars` bars back when it is lower than the `leftbars` values before it and the `rightbars` values after it, otherwise `na`.
signatures: ta.pivotlow(float source, int leftbars, int rightbars)

parameters.name: leftbars
parameters.description: Number of bars before the pivot that must be higher, at least 0.

parameters.name: rightbars
parameters.description: Number of bars after the pivot that must be higher, at least 0.

entries.returns: `float`: the pivot's value on the bar that reports it, otherwise `na`.
entries.body:
The pivot must be strictly lower than each of these `leftbars + rightbars`
neighbors: a tie with any of them is not a pivot. Neighbors that are `na`
are left out, but at least one must be known, unless `leftbars` and
`rightbars` are both `0`. A pivot is reported `rightbars` bars after its own
bar, so `bar_index - rightbars` is the bar index of the pivot.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{pivotlow}_t &=
\begin{cases}
p_t & \text{if } (J_t \ne \varnothing \lor n = 0)
\text{ and } \mathit{source}_{t-i} > p_t \text{ for every } i \in J_t \\
\text{na} & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases} \\
p_t &= \mathit{source}_{t-\mathit{rightbars}}, \qquad
n = \mathit{leftbars} + \mathit{rightbars} \\
J_t &= \{\, i : 0 \le i \le n,\ i \ne \mathit{rightbars},
\ \mathit{source}_{t-i} \ne \text{na} \,\}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` on the first `leftbars + rightbars` bars, so a value with fewer
than `leftbars` bars before it is never a pivot. After that, `na` on a bar
where the value `rightbars` bars back is `na`, or where that value has
neighbors and all of them are `na`.

**Example:** Two bars on each side, so the first four bars are `na` and the 7 at index 0,
with no bars before it, is never a pivot. Index 5 reports the 8 at index 3,
leaving out the missing low at index 4, and index 11 reports the 5 at index
9; the equal lows at indices 6 and 7 are not pivots.

```tea
emit "low" low
emit "pivotlow" ta.pivotlow(low, 2, 2)
```

```csv
time,low
0,7
1,9
2,10
3,8
4,
5,9
6,6
7,6
8,10
9,5
10,11
11,12
```

**Output:**

```text
index  low  pivotlow
0      7    na
1      9    na
2      10   na
3      8    na
4      na   na
5      9    8
6      6    na
7      6    na
8      10   na
9      5    na
10     11   na
11     12   5
```

**Pine Script:** Pine also has a two-argument form without `source`,
`ta.pivotlow(leftbars, rightbars)`; Tea always takes `source`. `leftbars`
and `rightbars` must be `int`, where Pine also accepts a `float`.

**See also:** [`ta.pivothigh`](#ta.pivothigh), [`ta.lowest`](#ta.lowest)

entries.summary: Cumulative sum: the running total of `source` over every bar so far.

parameters.name: source
parameters.description: Series to add up, such as [`volume`](#volume).

entries.returns: `float`: the sum of every known value of `source` so far.
entries.body:
Values that are `na` are left out: the total keeps its value on those bars.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{cum}_t &= \begin{cases}
\sum_{i \in K_t} \mathit{source}_{t-i} & \text{if } K_t \ne \varnothing \\
\text{na} & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases} \\
K_t &= \{\, i \ge 0 : \mathit{source}_{t-i} \ne \text{na} \,\}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` until the first bar where `source` is not `na`.

**Example:** The running total of volume. It is `na` until the first volume at index 1,
and the missing volume at index 4 leaves it at 400.

```tea
emit "volume" volume
emit "cum" ta.cum(volume)
```

```csv
time,volume
0,
1,100
2,200
3,100
4,
5,300
6,200
7,100
```

**Output:**

```text
index  volume  cum
0      na      na
1      100     100
2      200     300
3      100     400
4      na      400
5      300     700
6      200     900
7      100     1000
```

**See also:** [`ta.obv`](#ta.obv), [`ta.max`](#ta.max)

entries.summary: All-time high: the highest value of `source` on any bar so far.
entries.returns: `float`: the highest known value of `source` so far.
entries.body:
Values that are `na` are left out: the result keeps its value on those bars.
Compare [`ta.highest`](#ta.highest), which looks back a fixed number of bars.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{max}_t &= \max_{i \in K_t} \mathit{source}_{t-i} \\
K_t &= \{\, i \ge 0 : \mathit{source}_{t-i} \ne \text{na} \,\}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` until the first bar where `source` is not `na`.

**Example:** The highest high so far. It is `na` until the first high at index 1, and the
missing high at index 4 leaves it at 12.

```tea
emit "high" high
emit "max" ta.max(high)
```

```csv
time,high
0,
1,10
2,12
3,11
4,
5,14
6,13
7,15
```

**Output:**

```text
index  high  max
0      na    na
1      10    10
2      12    12
3      11    12
4      na    12
5      14    14
6      13    14
7      15    15
```

**See also:** [`ta.min`](#ta.min), [`ta.highest`](#ta.highest)

entries.summary: All-time low: the lowest value of `source` on any bar so far.
entries.returns: `float`: the lowest known value of `source` so far.
entries.body:
Values that are `na` are left out: the result keeps its value on those bars.
Compare [`ta.lowest`](#ta.lowest), which looks back a fixed number of bars.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{min}_t &= \min_{i \in K_t} \mathit{source}_{t-i} \\
K_t &= \{\, i \ge 0 : \mathit{source}_{t-i} \ne \text{na} \,\}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` until the first bar where `source` is not `na`.

**Example:** The lowest low so far. It is `na` until the first low at index 1, and the
missing low at index 4 leaves it at 8.

```tea
emit "low" low
emit "min" ta.min(low)
```

```csv
time,low
0,
1,10
2,8
3,9
4,
5,7
6,8
7,6
```

**Output:**

```text
index  low  min
0      na   na
1      10   10
2      8    8
3      9    8
4      na   8
5      7    7
6      8    7
7      6    6
```

**See also:** [`ta.max`](#ta.max), [`ta.lowest`](#ta.lowest)

entries.summary: Correlation coefficient of the last `length` values of `source1` and `source2`, from `-1` to `1`.
signatures: ta.correlation(float source1, float source2, int length)

parameters.name: source2
parameters.description: Second series, paired with `source1` bar by bar.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of bars in the window, at least 2.

entries.returns: `float`: Pearson's correlation coefficient, from `-1` to `1`.
entries.body:
It is Pearson's correlation of the values paired bar by bar. Pairs on a
rising straight line give `1` and pairs on a falling one give `-1`, up to
rounding; `0` means no straight-line relation. A bar where either value is
`na` is left out of both series.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{correlation}_t &= \max\left(-1,\ \min\left(1,
\ \frac{\sum_{i \in K_t} u_i v_i}
{\sqrt{\sum_{i \in K_t} u_i^2 \cdot \sum_{i \in K_t} v_i^2}}\right)\right) \\
u_i &= \mathit{source1}_{t-i}
- \frac{1}{|K_t|} \sum_{j \in K_t} \mathit{source1}_{t-j} \\
v_i &= \mathit{source2}_{t-i}
- \frac{1}{|K_t|} \sum_{j \in K_t} \mathit{source2}_{t-j} \\
K_t &= \{\, i : 0 \le i < \mathit{length},
\ \mathit{source1}_{t-i} \ne \text{na},
\ \mathit{source2}_{t-i} \ne \text{na} \,\}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` on the first `length - 1` bars, when fewer than two bars in the
window have both values, and when either series is constant over those bars.

**Example:** At index 2 the close and the volume both rise by equal steps, so the
correlation is 1; at index 4 the close falls by equal steps while the volume
rises, so it is -1. The volume is missing at index 7, so that window pairs
only its other two bars.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "volume" volume
emit "correlation" ta.correlation(close, volume, 3)
```

```csv
time,close,volume
0,10,100
1,11,200
2,12,300
3,11,400
4,10,500
5,11,400
6,12,300
7,13,
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  volume  correlation
0      10     100     na
1      11     200     na
2      12     300     1
3      11     400     0
4      10     500     -1
5      11     400     -1
6      12     300     -1
7      13     na      -1
```

**See also:** [`ta.variance`](#ta.variance), [`ta.stdev`](#ta.stdev)

entries.summary: Percent rank: the percentage of the previous `length` values of `source` that are less than or equal to its current value.

parameters.name: length
parameters.description: Number of previous values to compare with, at least 1.

entries.returns: `float`: a percentage from `0` to `100`, in steps of `100 / length`.
entries.body:
The current value is compared with the `length` values before it, not with
itself. An `na` value, current or previous, is not left out: it makes the
result `na`.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{percentrank}_t &= \begin{cases}
\text{na} & \text{if } \mathit{source}_{t-i} = \text{na}
\text{ for some } 0 \le i \le \mathit{length} \\
\dfrac{100}{\mathit{length}} \cdot |C_t| & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases} \\
\text{where}\quad C_t &= \{\, i : 1 \le i \le \mathit{length},
\ \mathit{source}_{t-i} \le \mathit{source}_t \,\}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` on the first `length` bars. An `na` value of `source` makes the
result `na` on its own bar and on the `length` bars after it.

**Example:** At index 5 the close 12 is greater than or equal to 11, 12 and 9 but not 13,
so it ranks 75. The missing close at index 6 makes the results at indexes 6
to 10 `na`, and at index 11 the close ranks again.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "rank" ta.percentrank(close, 4)
```

```csv
time,close
0,10
1,13
2,11
3,12
4,9
5,12
6,
7,14
8,8
9,12
10,13
11,11
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  rank
0      10     na
1      13     na
2      11     na
3      12     na
4      9      0
5      12     75
6      na     na
7      14     na
8      8      na
9      12     na
10     13     na
11     11     25
```

**See also:** [`ta.stoch`](#ta.stoch)

entries.summary: On-balance volume (OBV): the running total of [`volume`](#volume), added on bars where [`close`](#close) rose and subtracted on bars where it fell.
entries.body:
Each bar adds `math.sign(ta.change(close)) * volume`: its volume when the
close rose from the previous bar, minus its volume when it fell, and `0` when
it did not change. The total is in units of volume.

`ta.obv` is a variable, not a call: it is computed once per bar for the whole
script, so every read sees the same value, even one inside an `if`. The call
`ta.cum(math.sign(ta.change(close)) * volume)` gives the same value only
when it runs on every bar.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{obv}_t &= \sum_{s \in K_t} x_s
\quad (\text{na when } K_t \text{ is empty}) \\
x_s &= \operatorname{sign}(\mathit{close}_s - \mathit{close}_{s-1})
\cdot \mathit{volume}_s \\
K_t &= \{\, s \le t : x_s \ne \text{na} \,\}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` on the first bar, which has no previous close, and until the
first bar where `close`, the previous close and `volume` are all known. A
later bar where any of them is `na` leaves the total unchanged, so a missing
close holds it for two bars: its own and the next.

**Example:** OBV is `na` on the first bar and holds at index 3, where the close did not
change. The close is missing at index 5, so OBV holds there and at index 6.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "volume" volume
emit "obv" ta.obv
```

```csv
time,close,volume
0,10,100
1,11,200
2,10,150
3,10,300
4,12,250
5,,100
6,13,400
7,12,200
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  volume  obv
0      10     100     na
1      11     200     200
2      10     150     50
3      10     300     50
4      12     250     300
5      na     100     300
6      13     400     300
7      12     200     100
```

**Example:** The `if` reads `ta.obv` only from index 3 on, yet `late` equals `obv` there:
the variable counted the earlier bars too.

```tea
float late = na
if bar_index >= 3
    late := ta.obv
emit "close" close
emit "volume" volume
emit "obv" ta.obv
emit "late" late
```

```csv
time,close,volume
0,10,100
1,11,200
2,10,150
3,12,300
4,13,250
5,11,100
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  volume  obv  late
0      10     100     na   na
1      11     200     200  na
2      10     150     50   na
3      12     300     350  350
4      13     250     600  600
5      11     100     500  500
```

**See also:** [`ta.cum`](#ta.cum), [`ta.pvt`](#ta.pvt), [`ta.accdist`](#ta.accdist)

entries.summary: Accumulation/distribution (A/D): the running total of each bar's [`volume`](#volume), weighted by where [`close`](#close) sits between [`low`](#low) and [`high`](#high).
entries.body:
Each bar adds its [`ta.iii`](#ta.iii): `volume` when the close is at the high,
`-volume` when it is at the low and `0` at the midpoint. A bar where `high`
equals `low`, whose `ta.iii` is `na`, adds `0`. The total is in units of
volume. Like [`ta.obv`](#ta.obv), it is computed once per bar for the whole
script, wherever the script reads it.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{accdist}_t &= \sum_{s \in K_t} x_s
\quad (\text{na when } K_t \text{ is empty}) \\
x_s &= \begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } \mathit{high}_s = \mathit{low}_s \\
\dfrac{2\,\mathit{close}_s - \mathit{low}_s - \mathit{high}_s}
{\mathit{high}_s - \mathit{low}_s} \cdot \mathit{volume}_s
& \text{otherwise}
\end{cases} \\
K_t &= \{\, s \le t : x_s \ne \text{na} \,\}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` until a bar adds a value. A bar where `high` equals `low` adds
`0`; any other bar adds nothing while `close`, `high`, `low` or `volume` is
`na`, which leaves the total unchanged.

**Example:** Index 0 adds its volume, with the close at the high; index 1 subtracts its
volume, with the close at the low; index 2 adds `0`, with the close at the
midpoint. Index 4, where `high` equals `low`, adds `0`, and index 5, whose
close is missing, adds nothing.

```tea
emit "high" high
emit "low" low
emit "close" close
emit "volume" volume
emit "accdist" ta.accdist
```

```csv
time,high,low,close,volume
0,12,8,12,100
1,12,8,8,200
2,12,8,10,300
3,12,8,11,400
4,10,10,10,500
5,12,8,,100
6,14,10,13,200
```

**Output:**

```text
index  high  low  close  volume  accdist
0      12    8    12     100     100
1      12    8    8      200     -100
2      12    8    10     300     -100
3      12    8    11     400     100
4      10    10   10     500     100
5      12    8    na     100     100
6      14    10   13     200     200
```

**See also:** [`ta.iii`](#ta.iii), [`ta.obv`](#ta.obv), [`ta.cum`](#ta.cum)

entries.summary: Price-volume trend (PVT): the running total of each bar's [`volume`](#volume), weighted by the relative change of [`close`](#close).
entries.body:
Each bar adds `ta.change(close) / close[1] * volume`: its volume times the
fraction by which the close moved from the previous bar, so a 10% rise adds
a tenth of the volume. The total is in units of volume. Like
[`ta.obv`](#ta.obv), it is computed once per bar for the whole script, wherever
the script reads it.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{pvt}_t &= \sum_{s \in K_t} x_s
\quad (\text{na when } K_t \text{ is empty}) \\
x_s &= \frac{\mathit{close}_s - \mathit{close}_{s-1}}{\mathit{close}_{s-1}}
\cdot \mathit{volume}_s \\
K_t &= \{\, s \le t : x_s \ne \text{na} \,\}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** `na` on the first bar, which has no previous close, and until the
first bar where `close`, the previous close and `volume` are all known and
the previous close is not `0`. A later bar that fails this leaves the total
unchanged, so a missing close holds it for two bars: its own and the next.

**Example:** PVT is `na` on the first bar; at index 1 the close rises 10% and adds 20,
a tenth of the volume. The close is missing at index 5, so PVT holds there
and at index 6.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "volume" volume
emit "pvt" ta.pvt
```

```csv
time,close,volume
0,10,100
1,11,200
2,10,110
3,10,300
4,12,250
5,,100
6,15,400
7,12,200
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  volume  pvt
0      10     100     na
1      11     200     20
2      10     110     10
3      10     300     10
4      12     250     60
5      na     100     60
6      15     400     60
7      12     200     20
```

**See also:** [`ta.obv`](#ta.obv), [`ta.cum`](#ta.cum)

entries.summary: Intraday intensity index (III) of the current bar: where [`close`](#close) sits between [`low`](#low) and [`high`](#high), times [`volume`](#volume).
entries.body:
It is `volume` when the close is at the high, `-volume` when it is at the
low and `0` at the midpoint. It is not a running total; [`ta.accdist`](#ta.accdist)
adds it up.

**Formula**

$$
\mathrm{iii}_t = \frac
{2\,\mathit{close}_t - \mathit{high}_t - \mathit{low}_t}
{\mathit{high}_t - \mathit{low}_t} \cdot \mathit{volume}_t
$$

**Warm-up and na:** No warm-up: it has a value from the first bar. It is `na` on a bar
where `high` equals `low` or where `close`, `high`, `low` or `volume` is
`na`.

**Example:** The result is `volume` at index 0, where the close is at the high, `-volume`
at index 1, where it is at the low, and `0` at index 2, where it is at the
midpoint. It is `na` at index 4, where `high` equals `low`.

```tea
emit "high" high
emit "low" low
emit "close" close
emit "volume" volume
emit "iii" ta.iii
```

```csv
time,high,low,close,volume
0,12,8,12,100
1,12,8,8,200
2,12,8,10,300
3,12,8,11,400
4,10,10,10,500
5,14,10,13,200
```

**Output:**

```text
index  high  low  close  volume  iii
0      12    8    12     100     100
1      12    8    8      200     -200
2      12    8    10     300     0
3      12    8    11     400     200
4      10    10   10     500     na
5      14    10   13     200     100
```

**See also:** [`ta.accdist`](#ta.accdist), [`ta.wvad`](#ta.wvad)

entries.summary: Williams variable accumulation/distribution (WVAD) of the current bar: the move from [`open`](#open) to [`close`](#close) as a fraction of the bar's range, times [`volume`](#volume).
entries.body:
It is `volume` when the bar opens at its low and closes at its high, and
`-volume` when it opens at its high and closes at its low. It is not a
running total.

**Formula**

$$
\mathrm{wvad}_t = \frac{\mathit{close}_t - \mathit{open}_t}
{\mathit{high}_t - \mathit{low}_t} \cdot \mathit{volume}_t
$$

**Warm-up and na:** No warm-up: it has a value from the first bar. It is `na` on a bar
where `high` equals `low` or where `open`, `close`, `high`, `low` or
`volume` is `na`.

**Example:** Index 0 opens at its low and closes at its high, so the result is its
volume; index 1 does the opposite. The result is `na` at index 4, where
`high` equals `low`.

```tea
emit "open" open
emit "high" high
emit "low" low
emit "close" close
emit "volume" volume
emit "wvad" ta.wvad
```

```csv
time,open,high,low,close,volume
0,8,12,8,12,100
1,12,12,8,8,200
2,9,12,8,11,300
3,11,12,8,9,400
4,10,10,10,10,500
5,11,14,10,13,200
```

**Output:**

```text
index  open  high  low  close  volume  wvad
0      8     12    8    12     100     100
1      12    12    8    8      200     -200
2      9     12    8    11     300     150
3      11    12    8    9      400     -200
4      10    10    10   10     500     na
5      11    14    10   13     200     100
```

**See also:** [`ta.wad`](#ta.wad), [`ta.iii`](#ta.iii)

entries.summary: Williams accumulation/distribution (WAD): the running total of each bar's move from its true low on an up bar, or from its true high on a down bar.
entries.body:
The true low is the lower of [`low`](#low) and the previous [`close`](#close); the
true high is the higher of [`high`](#high) and the previous close. A bar whose
close rose adds `close` minus the true low, a bar whose close fell subtracts
the true high minus `close`, and a bar whose close did not change adds `0`.
The total is in price units; it does not use [`volume`](#volume). Like
[`ta.obv`](#ta.obv), it is computed once per bar for the whole script, wherever
the script reads it.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{wad}_t &= \sum_{s \in K_t} x_s,
\qquad K_t = \{\, s \le t : x_s \ne \text{na} \,\} \\
x_s &= \begin{cases}
\mathit{close}_s - \min(\mathit{low}_s, \mathit{close}_{s-1})
& \text{if } \mathit{close}_s > \mathit{close}_{s-1} \\
\mathit{close}_s - \max(\mathit{high}_s, \mathit{close}_{s-1})
& \text{if } \mathit{close}_s < \mathit{close}_{s-1} \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** Never `na`: it is `0` on the first bar, which has no previous close.
A bar adds `0` when `close` or the previous close is `na`, and when the
`low` of an up bar or the `high` of a down bar is `na`.

**Example:** At index 3 the previous close, 11, is below the low, so the bar adds
`14 - 11`; at index 5 the previous close, 14, is above the high, so the bar
subtracts `14 - 11`. The close is missing at index 6, so indexes 6 and 7
add `0`.

```tea
emit "high" high
emit "low" low
emit "close" close
emit "wad" ta.wad
```

```csv
time,high,low,close
0,11,9,10
1,13,10,12
2,12,9,11
3,15,12,14
4,14,12,14
5,13,10,11
6,13,11,
7,14,11,13
```

**Output:**

```text
index  high  low  close  wad
0      11    9    10     0
1      13    10   12     2
2      12    9    11     1
3      15    12   14     4
4      14    12   14     4
5      13    10   11     1
6      13    11   na     1
7      14    11   13     1
```

**See also:** [`ta.wvad`](#ta.wvad), [`ta.cum`](#ta.cum)

entries.summary: Negative volume index (NVI): starts at `1` and moves with [`close`](#close), by its relative change, only on bars whose [`volume`](#volume) fell from the previous bar.
entries.body:
On such a bar it changes by the same percentage as the close; on any other
bar it keeps its value. It is a ratio without a unit. [`ta.pvi`](#ta.pvi) moves on
the bars where volume rose, and a bar whose volume did not change moves
neither. Like [`ta.obv`](#ta.obv), it is computed once per bar for the whole
script, wherever the script reads it.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{nvi}_t &= \begin{cases}
\mathrm{nvi}_{t-1} + \dfrac{\mathit{close}_t - \mathit{close}_{t-1}}
{\mathit{close}_{t-1}} \cdot \mathrm{nvi}_{t-1} & \text{if } c_t \\
\mathrm{nvi}_{t-1} & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases} \\
\text{where}\quad c_t &= \big(\mathit{volume}_t < \operatorname{nz}(\mathit{volume}_{t-1})\big)
\land \big(\mathit{close}_t, \mathit{close}_{t-1} \notin \{0, \text{na}\}\big) \\
\mathrm{nvi} &= 1 \text{ before the first bar}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** Never `na`: it is `1` on the first bar. A bar leaves it unchanged
when `close` or the previous close is `na` or `0`, or when `volume` is `na`.
A previous `volume` that is `na` counts as `0`.

**Example:** NVI moves only where volume fell: down 25% with the close at index 2 and
down 50% at index 7. Volume is missing at index 5, so NVI holds there and at
index 6, where the missing volume counts as `0`.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "volume" volume
emit "nvi" ta.nvi
```

```csv
time,close,volume
0,8,100
1,12,200
2,9,100
3,9,100
4,18,150
5,12,
6,18,50
7,9,25
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  volume  nvi
0      8      100     1
1      12     200     1
2      9      100     0.75
3      9      100     0.75
4      18     150     0.75
5      12     na      0.75
6      18     50      0.75
7      9      25      0.375
```

**See also:** [`ta.pvi`](#ta.pvi), [`ta.obv`](#ta.obv)

entries.summary: Positive volume index (PVI): starts at `1` and moves with [`close`](#close), by its relative change, only on bars whose [`volume`](#volume) rose from the previous bar.
entries.body:
On such a bar it changes by the same percentage as the close; on any other
bar it keeps its value. It is a ratio without a unit. [`ta.nvi`](#ta.nvi) moves on
the bars where volume fell, and a bar whose volume did not change moves
neither. Like [`ta.obv`](#ta.obv), it is computed once per bar for the whole
script, wherever the script reads it.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{pvi}_t &= \begin{cases}
\mathrm{pvi}_{t-1} + \dfrac{\mathit{close}_t - \mathit{close}_{t-1}}
{\mathit{close}_{t-1}} \cdot \mathrm{pvi}_{t-1} & \text{if } c_t \\
\mathrm{pvi}_{t-1} & \text{otherwise}
\end{cases} \\
\text{where}\quad c_t &= \big(\mathit{volume}_t > \operatorname{nz}(\mathit{volume}_{t-1})\big)
\land \big(\mathit{close}_t, \mathit{close}_{t-1} \notin \{0, \text{na}\}\big) \\
\mathrm{pvi} &= 1 \text{ before the first bar}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Warm-up and na:** Never `na`: it is `1` on the first bar. A bar leaves it unchanged
when `close` or the previous close is `na` or `0`, or when `volume` is `na`.
A previous `volume` that is `na` counts as `0`.

**Example:** PVI moves only where volume rose: up 50% with the close at index 1 and up
100% at index 4. Volume is missing at index 5, so PVI holds there; at index 6
the missing volume counts as `0`, so PVI rises 50% with the close.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "volume" volume
emit "pvi" ta.pvi
```

```csv
time,close,volume
0,8,100
1,12,200
2,9,100
3,9,100
4,18,150
5,12,
6,18,50
7,9,25
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  volume  pvi
0      8      100     1
1      12     200     1.5
2      9      100     1.5
3      9      100     1.5
4      18     150     3
5      12     na      3
6      18     50      4.5
7      9      25      4.5
```

**See also:** [`ta.nvi`](#ta.nvi), [`ta.obv`](#ta.obv)

entries.summary: Spreads the volume of every bar since the last reset across price rows.
signatures:
ta.volumeProfile(
    array<float> highs,
    array<float> lows,
    array<float> volumes,
    array<bool> rising,
    bool reset,
    int rows = 24,
    float valueArea = 70.0,
    bool compute = true
)

parameters.name: highs
parameters.description: High of each bar added on this call.

parameters.name: lows
parameters.description: Low of each bar added on this call.

parameters.name: volumes
parameters.description: Volume of each bar added on this call.

parameters.name: rising
parameters.description: Whether each bar added on this call closed at or above its open.

parameters.name: reset
parameters.description: Whether to finish the current profile, returning it, and start a new one with this call's bars.

parameters.name: rows
parameters.description: Number of price rows, a positive `int`.

parameters.name: valueArea
parameters.description: Share of the volume, in percent, that the value area holds.

parameters.name: compute
parameters.description: Whether to build the profile this call returns; `false` returns an empty profile.

entries.returns: The finished profile on a reset, else the profile so far.
entries.body:
Each call adds a group of bars, such as the lower-timeframe bars inside the
current chart bar from [`request.security_lower_tf`](#request.security_lower_tf). The range from the
lowest low to the highest high is cut into `rows` equal rows. Each bar's
volume is spread over the rows its low-to-high range covers, in proportion to
the overlap; a bar whose high equals its low puts all its volume in one row.
The value area grows from the point of control one row at a time, taking the
neighbor with more volume (the upper one on a tie), until it holds
`valueArea` percent of the volume.

Volume is kept in four fine cells per row, so a call costs only the cells
its bars touch. Rows are built from the cells, which splits a cell lying
across a row boundary in proportion: a row can differ from an exact split
by part of one cell's volume, and the total never changes. Building the rows
is the costly part, so pass `compute = false` on bars that do not need the
profile; their bars still count.

With `reset`, the call returns the profile that just finished, of every bar
before this call, and this call's bars start the next one. A period's profile
is therefore ready on the first bar of the next period. The four arrays
describe the same bars in the same order; bars with an `na` high or low are
skipped and an `na` volume counts as `0`. To profile every bar of the chart,
pass one-element arrays and never reset:

```tea
profile = ta.volumeProfile(array.from(high), array.from(low), array.from(volume), array.from(close >= open), false)
emit "poc" profile.low + (profile.poc + 0.5) * profile.step
```

entries.summary: Volume traded at each price over a range of bars, as returned by [`ta.volumeProfile`](#ta.volumeProfile).

rows: Bottom of the first row: the lowest low counted.
Volume of rising bars, those closing at or above their open, in each row.
Volume of falling bars in each row.
Row with the most volume, the point of control; the lowest such row on a tie.
Lowest row of the value area.
Highest row of the value area.

entries.body:
Row `i` covers the prices from `low + i * step` to `low + (i + 1) * step`.
The arrays hold one value per row, the bottom row first. An empty profile,
when the window holds no bar with a price range, has no rows and is `na`
everywhere else.

pages.title: Core functions
pages.description: Missing values, conversions, script declarations and script errors.
pages.intro: Functions available in every script without an import.

entries.summary: Declares a file as a library and names it.

parameters.name: title
parameters.description: The library’s name, which importing scripts use as its namespace. It must be an identifier: letters, digits and underscores, not starting with a digit, and not a keyword. Must be a compile-time constant.

entries.body:
It must be the file’s first statement and appear only once. A script that imports the file uses this name unless it renames the import with `as`. See [Imports](#imports).

```tea
library("bands")

export upper(float source, float width) => source + width
```

entries.summary: Declares the script’s title and whether a host draws it over the price chart.
signatures: void indicator(const string title, const bool overlay = …)

parameters.name: title
parameters.description: The name a host shows for the script. It cannot be empty. Must be a compile-time constant. Cannot be `na`.

parameters.name: overlay
parameters.description: `true` to draw the script’s outputs over the price chart; `false`, the default, to draw them in a separate pane. Pass it by name, as `overlay = true`: the second position belongs to `shorttitle`, which Tea does not accept yet, so `indicator("X", true)` is an error. Must be a compile-time constant.

entries.body:
It must be the script’s first statement and appear at most once, and a library cannot declare it. The header only informs the host; it never changes how the script runs.

**Example:** The header changes nothing in the output: `range` is `high - low` on every bar, from 2 on bar 0 to 5 on bar 5.

```tea
indicator("Bar range", overlay = false)
emit "high" high
emit "low" low
emit "range" high - low
```

```csv
time,high,low
0,10,8
1,12,9
2,11,7
3,13,9
4,12,8
5,15,10
```

**Output:**

```text
index  high  low  range
0      10    8    2
1      12    9    3
2      11    7    4
3      13    9    4
4      12    8    4
5      15    10   5
```

entries.summary: Tests whether a value is missing.

parameters.name: x
parameters.description: The value to test. It can have any type except `bool`, which is never missing.

entries.returns: `true` when `x` is `na`, otherwise `false`.
entries.body:
Every comparison involving a missing value is `false`, even `!=`, and `x == na` is a compile error, so test with `na(x)`. Arithmetic without a defined result, such as division by zero or the square root of a negative number, gives `na`. An `na` array, matrix or map is no collection at all, unlike an empty one, and an `na` struct refers to no struct.

**Example:** Bar 0 has no previous close, so `previous` is `na` and `missing` is `true` there; on every later bar `missing` is `false`.

```tea
previous = close[1]
emit "close" close
emit "previous" previous
emit "missing" na(previous)
```

```csv
time,close
0,9
1,12
2,12
3,15
4,12
5,18
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  previous  missing
0      9      na        true
1      12     9         false
2      12     12        false
3      15     12        false
4      12     15        false
5      18     12        false
```

**See also:** [`nz`](#nz)

entries.summary: Replaces a missing value with a fallback.
signatures: int nz(series int source, series int replacement = …)
float nz(series float source, series float replacement = …)
color nz(series color source, series color replacement = …)

parameters.name: source
parameters.type: series int, series float, series color

parameters.name: replacement
parameters.type: series int, series float, series color
parameters.description: The value to use when `source` is `na`. Without it, the fallback is `0` for numbers and fully transparent black (`#00000000`) for colors.

entries.returns: `source` when it is not `na`, otherwise the replacement.
entries.body:
**Example:** On bar 0, `change` is `na`: `filled` replaces it with 0, and `previous` falls back to that bar’s own close, 9.

```tea
change = close - close[1]
emit "close" close
emit "change" change
emit "filled" nz(change)
emit "previous" nz(close[1], close)
```

```csv
time,close
0,9
1,12
2,12
3,15
4,12
5,18
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  change  filled  previous
0      9      na      0       9
1      12     3       3       9
2      12     0       0       12
3      15     3       3       12
4      12     -3      -3      15
5      18     6       6       12
```

**See also:** [`na`](#na)

entries.summary: Converts a number to an integer by dropping its fractional part.
entries.returns: `x` truncated toward zero, so `int(-2.7)` is `-2`; `na` when `x` is `na`.
entries.body:
**Example:** `int` drops the fraction toward zero, so `negative` is `-2`, while `math.round(-2.7)` is `-3`.

```tea
emit "positive" int(2.7)
emit "negative" int(-2.7)
emit "rounded" math.round(-2.7)
```

**Output:**

```text
index  positive  negative  rounded
0      2         -2        -3
```

**See also:** [`math.round`](#math.round), [`math.floor`](#math.floor), [`float`](#float)

entries.summary: Converts a number to a `float`.
entries.returns: `x` as a `float`; `na` when `x` is `na`.
entries.body:
Dividing one `int` by another truncates, so convert one of them to keep the fraction. `float(na)` is a missing value of type `float`; use it where a bare `na` has no type, such as a request expression.

**Example:** Both operands of `7 / 2` are `int`, so `ints` is truncated to 3; converting one to `float` keeps the fraction.

```tea
emit "ints" 7 / 2
emit "floats" float(7) / 2
```

**Output:**

```text
index  ints  floats
0      3     3.5
```

**See also:** [`int`](#int)

entries.summary: Converts a value to text.
signatures: string str.tostring(series scalar | enum | resource value)
entries.returns: The text form of `value`; `"NaN"` when `value` is `na`.
entries.body:
Numbers use the shortest form that reads back as the same number: `3.0` gives `"3"`, `0.1 + 0.2` gives `"0.30000000000000004"`, and very large or small numbers use exponent notation such as `"1e+21"`. There is no format argument; round with [`math.round`](#math.round) first to limit the decimals. A `string` is returned unchanged, a `bool` gives `"true"` or `"false"`, a color its hex code such as `"#FF5252"` (with two more digits when it is transparent), and an enum member its title, or its name when it has no title.

**Example:** `3.0` prints as `3`, the sum keeps every digit until `math.round` limits it, a transparent color gets two more hex digits for its opacity, and `na` prints as `NaN`.

```tea
emit "number" str.tostring(3.0)
emit "sum" str.tostring(0.1 + 0.2)
emit "rounded" str.tostring(math.round(0.1 + 0.2, 2))
emit "flag" str.tostring(1 < 2)
emit "color" str.tostring(color.new(color.red, 80))
emit "missing" str.tostring(float(na))
```

**Output:**

```text
index  number  sum                  rounded  flag  color      missing
0      3       0.30000000000000004  0.3      true  #FF525233  NaN
```

**Pine Script:** Tea has no `format` argument and does not convert arrays.

**See also:** [`math.round`](#math.round)

entries.summary: Stops the script with an error message.
entries.body:
When a call runs, the run stops: no output is published for that bar or any later one, and the host receives the message.

A call that runs every time its script or function runs is a compile error instead: one with no `if` around it, or only `if`s whose constant conditions select it. Constant arguments count as constants inside the function they are passed to, so `ta.sma(close, 0)` is rejected where it is written, even inside an `if`. A call inside a loop, inside a `switch`, or after a `return` that may run first is only checked when it runs.

This script stops on its first bar when the host sets `length` below 2:

```tea
length = input.int(14)
if length < 2
    runtime.error("length must be at least 2")
emit "average" ta.sma(close, length)
```

**Pine Script:** A call that runs every time its script or function runs is rejected when the script compiles, instead of stopping the run.

pages.title: math
pages.description: Arithmetic helpers and mathematical constants.
pages.intro: Functions and constants in the `math` namespace.

entries.summary: Returns the absolute value of a number.
entries.returns: `number` without its sign, with the same type; `na` when it is `na`.
entries.body:
**Example:** `size` is `change` without its sign, so bar 4’s `-3` becomes 3; both are `na` on bar 0.

```tea
change = close - close[1]
emit "close" close
emit "change" change
emit "size" math.abs(change)
```

```csv
time,close
0,9
1,12
2,12
3,15
4,12
5,18
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  change  size
0      9      na      na
1      12     3       3
2      12     0       0
3      15     3       3
4      12     -3      3
5      18     6       6
```

**See also:** [`math.sign`](#math.sign)

entries.summary: Returns the sign of a number as -1, 0 or 1.
entries.returns: `-1` for a negative number, `1` for a positive one and `0` for zero, with the type of `number`; `na` when it is `na`.
entries.body:
**Example:** `direction` is 1 where the close rose, -1 on bar 4, where it fell, and 0 on bar 2, where it did not change.

```tea
emit "close" close
emit "direction" math.sign(close - close[1])
```

```csv
time,close
0,9
1,12
2,12
3,15
4,12
5,18
```

**Output:**

```text
index  close  direction
0      9      na
1      12     1
2      12     0
3      15     1
4      12     -1
5      18     1
```

**See also:** [`math.abs`](#math.abs)

entries.summary: Rounds a number down to an integer.
entries.returns: The largest integer that is not greater than `number`; `na` when it is `na`.
entries.body:
**Example:** Rounding down goes toward negative infinity, so `negative` is `-3`, while `int(-2.7)` is `-2`.

```tea
emit "positive" math.floor(2.7)
emit "negative" math.floor(-2.7)
```

**Output:**

```text
index  positive  negative
0      2         -3
```

**See also:** [`math.ceil`](#math.ceil), [`math.round`](#math.round), [`int`](#int)

entries.summary: Rounds a number up to an integer.
entries.returns: The smallest integer that is not less than `number`; `na` when it is `na`.
entries.body:
**Example:** Rounding up goes toward positive infinity, so `positive` is 3 and `negative` is `-2`.

```tea
emit "positive" math.ceil(2.2)
emit "negative" math.ceil(-2.7)
```

**Output:**

```text
index  positive  negative
0      3         -2
```

**See also:** [`math.floor`](#math.floor), [`math.round`](#math.round)

entries.summary: Rounds a number to the nearest integer, or to a number of decimal places.
signatures:
float math.round(
    series int | float number,
    series int precision
)

parameters.name: precision
parameters.description: How many decimal places to keep. A negative value rounds to tens, hundreds and so on.

entries.returns: An `int` without `precision` and a `float` with it; `na` when an argument is `na`.
entries.body:
Halves round up, toward positive infinity: `math.round(2.5)` is `3` and `math.round(-2.5)` is `-2`. With `precision`, the product of `number` and 10 to the power `precision` is computed in binary floating point before it is rounded, so the result can differ from decimal arithmetic: `math.round(2.675, 2)` is `2.68`, because `2.675 * 100` gives exactly `267.5`, but `math.round(1.005, 2)` is `1`, because `1.005 * 100` gives slightly less than `100.5`. The result is `na` when that product, or 10 to the power `precision`, is too large to represent, as for any `precision` above 308. It is also `na` for a `precision` below -323, where 10 to the power `precision` is too small to represent.

**Formula**

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{round}(\mathit{number}) &= \left\lfloor \mathit{number} + \tfrac{1}{2} \right\rfloor \\
\operatorname{round}(\mathit{number}, \mathit{precision}) &= \left\lfloor \mathit{number} \cdot 10^{\mathit{precision}} + \tfrac{1}{2} \right\rfloor / 10^{\mathit{precision}}
\end{aligned}
$$

**Example:** Halves round up, so `negative_half` is `-2`; `cents` is 2.68 because `2.675 * 100` computes to exactly 267.5, but `below_half` is 1 because `1.005 * 100` computes to just under 100.5. 10 to the power 400 is too large, so `overflow` is `na`.

```tea
emit "half" math.round(2.5)
emit "negative_half" math.round(-2.5)
emit "cents" math.round(2.675, 2)
emit "below_half" math.round(1.005, 2)
emit "hundreds" math.round(1234.5, -2)
emit "overflow" math.round(2.5, 400)
```

**Output:**

```text
index  half  negative_half  cents  below_half  hundreds  overflow
0      3     -2             2.68   1           1200      na
```

**See also:** [`math.floor`](#math.floor), [`math.ceil`](#math.ceil), [`str.tostring`](#str.tostring)

entries.summary: Returns the square root of a number.
entries.returns: The square root; `na` when `number` is negative or `na`.
entries.body:
**Example:** A negative number has no real square root, so `negative` is `na`.

```tea
emit "root" math.sqrt(16)
emit "negative" math.sqrt(-4)
```

**Output:**

```text
index  root  negative
0      4     na
```

**See also:** [`math.pow`](#math.pow)

entries.summary: Raises a number to a power.
signatures:
float math.pow(
    series int | float base,
    series int | float exponent
)
entries.returns: `base` raised to `exponent`; `na` when an argument is `na` or the result is not a finite real number, such as a negative base with a fractional exponent.
entries.body:
**Example:** An exponent of `1.0 / 3` takes a cube root. A negative base with a fractional exponent has no real result, and an `na` base gives `na` even with the exponent 0.

```tea
emit "power" math.pow(2, 10)
emit "cube_root" math.pow(27, 1.0 / 3)
emit "negative_base" math.pow(-8, 1.0 / 3)
emit "missing" math.pow(float(na), 0)
```

**Output:**

```text
index  power  cube_root  negative_base  missing
0      1024   3          na             na
```

**See also:** [`math.sqrt`](#math.sqrt), [`math.exp`](#math.exp)

entries.summary: Returns the natural logarithm of a number.
entries.returns: The base-e logarithm; `na` when `number` is zero, negative or `na`.
entries.body:
**Example:** The natural logarithm of `math.e` is 1; zero has no logarithm, so `zero` is `na`.

```tea
emit "one" math.log(math.e)
emit "zero" math.log(0)
```

**Output:**

```text
index  one  zero
0      1    na
```

**See also:** [`math.log10`](#math.log10), [`math.exp`](#math.exp)

entries.summary: Returns the base-10 logarithm of a number.
entries.returns: The base-10 logarithm; `na` when `number` is zero, negative or `na`.
entries.body:
**Example:** `thousand` is 3, since 10 to the power 3 is 1000; a negative number has no logarithm, so `negative` is `na`.

```tea
emit "thousand" math.log10(1000)
emit "negative" math.log10(-1)
```

**Output:**

```text
index  thousand  negative
0      3         na
```

**See also:** [`math.log`](#math.log)

entries.summary: Returns e raised to a power.
entries.returns: e to the power `number`; `na` when `number` is `na` or the result is too large to represent.
entries.body:
**Example:** `one` is e itself; e to the power 1000 is too large to represent, so `large` is `na`.

```tea
emit "one" math.exp(1)
emit "large" math.exp(1000)
```

**Output:**

```text
index  one                large
0      2.718281828459045  na
```

**See also:** [`math.log`](#math.log), [`math.e`](#math.e)

entries.summary: Returns the average of its arguments.

parameters.name: number
parameters.description: The numbers to average; at least one.

entries.returns: Their arithmetic mean; `na` when any argument is `na`.
entries.body:
**Formula**

$$
\operatorname{avg}(x_1, \dots, x_n) = \frac{x_1 + \dots + x_n}{n}
$$

**Example:** `middle` is halfway between each bar’s open and close, such as 9.5 on bar 0.

```tea
emit "open" open
emit "close" close
emit "middle" math.avg(open, close)
```

```csv
time,open,close
0,10,9
1,9,12
2,12,12
3,12,15
4,15,12
5,12,18
```

**Output:**

```text
index  open  close  middle
0      10    9      9.5
1      9     12     10.5
2      12    12     12
3      12    15     13.5
4      15    12     13.5
5      12    18     15
```

**See also:** [`math.max`](#math.max), [`math.min`](#math.min), [`ta.sma`](#ta.sma)
